title: Five ways to build an animal: sponges, stingers, shells, armour and stars, and the octopus with three hearts and clever arms

summary.text: An octopus has three hearts and most of her nerve cells in her arms. So who is in charge, her brain or her arms? In this unit you will sort animals without backbones into five groups, and test with a coin and chana whether a hand works better when ordered or left to feel.
summary.art: An octopus on a rock with one arm inside a crack, beside a snail, a sponge, a coral, a crab and a starfish on the same sea floor.

intro.hook: Shut your eyes and do up a shirt button. Your fingers find the hole and push the button through. Did you tell each finger where to bend?
intro.text: You did not. You only decided to do up the button, and your hand did the rest by feel. An octopus has eight arms with no bones, and each arm can bend at any point along its length. Could one brain give orders for every bend of all eight arms at once? In this unit you meet five big groups of animals without backbones. Each group runs a body in a different way. Then you test how the octopus might share the work between her brain and her arms.
intro.art: A child with her eyes shut doing up a shirt button, and beside her a small octopus reaching one arm into a glass jar.

outcomes: I can name the five big groups of animals without backbones in this unit, and give one body clue for each group.
I can explain how a sponge feeds with no mouth, no gut and no nerve cells, and why a sponge is still an animal.
I can explain how a stinging cell fires, and how coral animals build a reef.
I can describe the body plan of a mollusc, and say how an octopus fits that plan.
I can say why arthropods have so many kinds, how an echinoderm moves by water power, and why a starfish is a closer relative of mine than a crab is.
I can explain why an octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
I can run a fair test of two ways to control a hand, and use the results to explain how an octopus shares work between her brain and her arms.
I can compare how messages travel in a sponge, a jellyfish, a starfish, an insect and an octopus, and explain what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: A very big group of animals who share one basic body layout. The plural is phyla.
terms.example: Snails, clams and octopuses all belong to the phylum of molluscs.
terms.art: Five large circles on a page, each holding small drawings of animals of one group.

terms.meaning: Many cells of the same kind that are joined together and do one job.
terms.example: Muscle is a tissue. A sponge has cells but no true tissues.
terms.art: A close-up of a sheet of muscle cells lying side by side, next to a few loose sponge cells.

terms.meaning: A body part made of several tissues that work together on one job.
terms.example: A heart, a gill and an eye are organs.
terms.art: A simple drawing of an octopus with the three hearts, the gills and one eye outlined.

terms.meaning: An animal who feeds by straining tiny bits of food out of water.
terms.example: A sponge, a mussel and a barnacle are filter feeders.
terms.art: A mussel on a rock with the two shells slightly open and small specks drifting in.

terms.meaning: A cell lining the inside of a sponge. It has one whip-like thread that beats, and a ring of tiny fingers that catches food.
terms.example: Millions of collar cells beating together pull water through a sponge.
terms.art: One cell with a long thread sticking out of a ring of short fingers, with specks caught on the ring.

terms.meaning: The large opening at the top of a sponge, where the filtered water flows out.
terms.example: Water enters a sponge by thousands of small pores and leaves by the osculum.
terms.art: A vase-shaped sponge with arrows going in at the sides and one arrow coming out of the wide opening at the top.

terms.meaning: A tiny hard needle or star inside a sponge. Spicules are made of glass-like silica or of chalky calcium carbonate.
terms.example: Thousands of spicules make up the skeleton of many sponges.
terms.art: A handful of tiny glassy needles and three-pointed stars seen under a magnifying glass.

terms.meaning: An animal with a soft body in two layers, one opening and stinging cells. You say it 'nye-DAIR-ee-an'.
terms.example: Jellyfish, corals, sea anemones and hydras are cnidarians.
terms.art: A jellyfish, a sea anemone and a branch of coral side by side.

terms.meaning: The tiny capsule inside a stinging cell. It holds a coiled hollow thread that shoots out when touched.
terms.example: A jellyfish tentacle carries thousands of nematocysts.
terms.art: A small capsule with a coiled thread inside, and next to it the same capsule with the thread shot out straight.

terms.meaning: Nerve cells spread through a body like a net, with no brain.
terms.example: A jellyfish and a sea anemone each have a nerve net.
terms.art: The outline of a sea anemone with a fine net of lines running all through the body.

terms.meaning: The fold of skin that covers a mollusc's soft body. In most molluscs the mantle makes the shell.
terms.example: A snail's mantle adds new shell at the opening as the snail grows.
terms.art: A snail drawn in cross-section with the fold of skin under the shell shaded.

terms.meaning: A ribbon in a mollusc's mouth covered with rows of tiny teeth, used for scraping or cutting food.
terms.example: A garden snail scrapes a leaf with a radula. An octopus has one behind her beak.
terms.art: A close-up of a ribbon with rows of tiny hooked teeth scraping the surface of a leaf.

terms.meaning: A mollusc with a large head and a ring of arms around the mouth. The word means 'head-foot'.
terms.example: Octopuses, squid, cuttlefish and the nautilus are cephalopods.
terms.art: An octopus, a squid and a cuttlefish swimming in a row.

terms.meaning: A leg or other limb made of stiff pieces that bend only where the pieces meet.
terms.example: A crab's leg and an ant's leg are jointed limbs.
terms.art: A crab's leg drawn large, with small arrows at each of its bending points.

terms.meaning: A sea animal with a body in five matching parts, chalky plates in the skin, and tube feet. You say it 'eh-KY-no-derm'.
terms.example: Starfish, sea urchins, brittle stars and sea cucumbers are echinoderms.
terms.art: A starfish, a sea urchin and a sea cucumber on sand.

terms.meaning: The set of water-filled canals inside an echinoderm. Muscles squeeze the water to push the tube feet out.
terms.example: A starfish walks by pushing water into hundreds of tube feet.
terms.art: A starfish seen from above with a ring canal and five canals drawn inside, each lined with small tube feet.

terms.meaning: A knot of nerve cells packed close together. The plural is ganglia.
terms.example: An octopus arm has a ganglion beside every sucker.
terms.art: A cord with small round knots along it, each knot joined by fine lines to a sucker.

terms.meaning: A thick bundle of nerve cells and nerve fibres that runs along a body or a limb.
terms.example: A nerve cord runs down the middle of each octopus arm.
terms.art: An octopus arm cut across, showing a round cord in the centre surrounded by muscle.

terms.meaning: The substance that carries oxygen in the blood of octopuses, snails, crabs and spiders. It holds copper, and it is blue when it carries oxygen.
terms.example: Haemocyanin makes an octopus's blood blue.
terms.art: A drop of blue blood beside a drop of red blood, with a tiny copper coin under the blue and an iron nail under the red.

terms.meaning: One of the two small hearts of an octopus. Each one pushes blood through one gill. Scientists call it a branchial heart.
terms.example: The two gill hearts send blood through the gills before the main heart sends it round the body.
terms.art: An octopus body in outline with two small hearts, each at the base of a feathery gill, and one larger heart between them.

explanations.concept: A phylum is a big group of animals built on one body plan
explanations.description: 'Invertebrate' only says what an animal lacks, which is a backbone. It does not say what the animal has. So scientists sort animals by how the body is built. A body plan is the basic layout of a body: how many layers, how many openings, what holds the body up and where the nerve cells are. Animals who share a body plan are put in one phylum. Why does the plan matter more than the look? A body plan is passed down from parents to young over hundreds of millions of years, while size, colour and home change much faster. So a shared plan is a sign of shared ancestors. Scientists count about 35 phyla of animals. This unit visits five of them: sponges, cnidarians, molluscs, arthropods and echinoderms. Animals with backbones are only part of one more phylum, the chordates. Earthworms belong to yet another, the segmented worms.
examples: A cuttlefish looks like a fish, but her body plan is a mollusc's, so she is grouped with snails.
A barnacle on a rock looks like a small shellfish. As a baby the barnacle swims with jointed legs, so barnacles are arthropods.
A whale and a mouse look very different, yet both are chordates, in the same phylum as you.
explanations.art: A page with six labelled circles: sponges, cnidarians, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms and chordates, each with two or three small animals inside.
explanations.definition: A phylum is a very large group of animals who share the same basic body layout, because they all come from the same ancestors.

explanations.concept: Sponges: a body of cells with no mouth, gut, muscles or nerve cells
explanations.description: A sponge sits fixed to a rock and never chases food. So how does a sponge eat? The inside canals are lined with collar cells. Each collar cell beats one whip-like thread, and millions of threads together pull water in through thousands of small pores. A ring of tiny fingers on each collar cell catches bacteria and other specks of food. Other cells crawl through the body and carry the food around. The used water leaves through a large opening called the osculum. Why one big exit? The water shoots out in a strong jet and travels far away, so the sponge does not take in the same used water again. A sponge has no mouth, no gut, no heart, no muscles and no nerve cells. A sponge is still an animal, because a sponge is made of many cells, eats other living things, and makes eggs and sperm. Over 9,000 kinds have been named. Nearly all live in the sea, and a few live in lakes and rivers.
examples: Measured sponges pump between about a third of their own volume and 35 times their own volume of water every minute.
Sponges take out between three quarters and nearly all of the bacteria in the water that passes through them.
The old bath sponge is the soft skeleton of a sea sponge. Most 'sponges' in shops today are made in factories, and a loofah is the dried fruit of a climbing plant.
explanations.art: A vase-shaped sponge cut open to show canals, with small arrows entering through the side wall and one large arrow leaving at the top.
explanations.definition: A sponge is an animal whose body is a wall of cells around water canals. Water flows in through many small pores and out through one or a few large openings.

explanations.concept: How a sponge acts as one body without nerve cells
explanations.description: A sponge acts as one body, with no nerve cells to carry messages. Dirt that is too big to eat gets trapped in slime on the sponge's surface. Every few hours the whole sponge slowly squeezes and relaxes, and the slime comes loose with the dirt. In 2022, Niklas Kornder and his team filmed tube sponges in the Caribbean doing this. Each squeeze took about half an hour, and they called it a sneeze. How do cells far apart act together? Scientists think one cell lets out a chemical, the next cell senses that chemical and lets out more, and so the signal spreads slowly from cell to cell. The details are still being worked out. Sponge cells also know their own body. In 1907, Henry Van Peters Wilson pressed a red sponge through fine cloth until the sponge was a cloud of loose cells. The cells crawled together into clumps, and in a few weeks the clumps had grown into small working sponges. When he mixed the cells of two kinds of sponge, the cells sorted themselves out by kind.
examples: A sponge sneeze starts every three to eight hours and lasts about half an hour.
Sally Leys and her students in Canada filmed a small freshwater sponge doing the same slow squeeze in a dish in the laboratory.
Your own cells also signal each other with chemicals. Hormones in your blood work this way.

perspectives.who: Sally Leys and other sponge scientists
perspectives.explanation: Sponge cells pass chemical signals to their neighbours, and that is enough to make the whole body squeeze together. Sponges have many of the genes that other animals use in nerve cells, although they have no nerve cells.
Nobody has traced the whole path of the signal from the first cell to the last. Scientists also do not agree on whether the ancestors of sponges once had nerve cells and lost them.

explanations.art: A tube sponge shown three times in a row: relaxed, squeezed thin with strings of mucus leaving the surface, and relaxed again.

explanations.concept: Cnidarians: two layers, one opening and stinging cells
explanations.description: Jellyfish, sea anemones, corals and the tiny freshwater hydra are cnidarians. More than 10,000 kinds have been named. Unlike a sponge, a cnidarian has true tissues, a mouth and a stomach space. Food goes in through the one opening, and what cannot be digested comes out the same way. A cnidarian also has muscle cells and nerve cells. The nerve cells are spread through the body as a nerve net, with no brain. So a touch on one side of a sea anemone spreads through the net, and the whole animal closes. What sets this phylum apart is the stinging cell. Each one holds a capsule called a nematocyst, with a hollow thread coiled inside and squeezed under very high pressure. A touch opens the lid. The thread turns inside out and shoots into the prey. In 2006, Timm Nüchter and his team in Germany filmed this in a hydra. It took about 700 billionths of a second, which is one of the fastest movements known in any animal.
examples: A bluebottle on a beach in Mumbai or Goa can still sting after being washed up, because each nematocyst fires by itself when touched.
A sea anemone and a jellyfish have the same plan. The anemone sits mouth up, and the jellyfish swims mouth down.
A used nematocyst cannot be loaded again. The animal grows a new stinging cell to replace it.
explanations.art: A jellyfish tentacle touching a tiny shrimp, with a zoom-in circle showing a capsule firing a thread into the shrimp.
explanations.definition: A cnidarian is an animal with a soft body built in two layers, one opening that serves as both mouth and exit, and stinging cells.

explanations.concept: Corals: tiny animals who build reefs
explanations.description: A coral looks like a rock or a plant, but each small bump is an animal called a polyp, with a ring of stinging tentacles around a mouth. A polyp takes calcium and carbon dissolved in sea water and builds a cup of limestone. Polyps divide and stay joined, so one colony can hold many thousands of them, all linked by a thin sheet of living tissue that shares food. Why do reefs grow only in clear, shallow, warm water? Inside the cells of reef corals live tiny algae. The algae use sunlight to make sugar and pass most of the sugar to the coral. The coral gives them shelter and the waste that they use as fertiliser. When the sea stays too warm for weeks, this partnership breaks down and the algae leave or are pushed out. The coral turns white. This is called bleaching. A bleached coral is alive but hungry, and dies if the heat lasts too long.
examples: India's coral reefs are in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
The islands of Lakshadweep are atolls. Each one is built from the limestone of corals.
Corals also catch tiny animals with their tentacles, mostly at night.
explanations.art: A piece of coral with a zoom-in showing a single polyp sitting in a stony cup, with small green dots inside the polyp's body.
explanations.definition: A coral is a colony of small cnidarians called polyps. Each polyp builds a cup of limestone under their body, and the cups of many generations make a reef.

explanations.concept: Molluscs: a soft body, a mantle, a foot and a toothed ribbon
explanations.description: Snails, slugs, clams, mussels, oysters, squid, cuttlefish and octopuses are all molluscs. Tens of thousands of kinds have been named, more than in any phylum except the arthropods. How can a snail and an octopus belong together? They share four parts. The mantle is a fold of skin over the body, and in most molluscs the mantle lays down the shell, layer by layer, from calcium and carbon in the water or food. The foot is a thick muscle used for creeping or digging. The radula is a ribbon of tiny teeth in the mouth. And unlike a sponge or a jellyfish, a mollusc has organs: a heart, gills or a lung, a gut with two ends, and knots of nerve cells called ganglia. Each group uses the plan in a different way. A snail creeps on the foot and scrapes with the radula. A mussel has two shells, no head and no radula, and filters food from water with large gills.
examples: The sacred chank, the sangu blown in temples, is the shell of a large sea snail. Divers collect chanks in the Gulf of Mannar near Thoothukudi.
A pearl forms when an oyster's mantle coats something stuck inside the shell with the same shiny layers that line the shell.
Green mussels, called kallumakkaya in Kerala, are molluscs with two shells.
explanations.art: A snail, a mussel and an octopus in a row, each with the mantle shaded in one colour and the foot in another.
explanations.definition: A mollusc is an animal with a soft body that is not divided into segments, covered by a fold of skin called the mantle. Most molluscs have a muscular foot, a shell and a radula.

explanations.concept: Arthropods: armour, segments and jointed limbs
explanations.description: Insects, spiders, scorpions, crabs, prawns, centipedes and millipedes are arthropods. More than a million kinds have been named. That is about four out of every five kinds of animal known. Why so many? One reason is the body plan. The body is a row of segments, and each segment can carry a pair of jointed limbs. Over a very long time, limbs on different segments have changed shape and taken different jobs. A prawn has 19 pairs of limbs. Some are feelers, some are jaws, some hold food, some are legs for walking, some are paddles, and the last pair makes the tail fan. An insect's jaws and feelers are also changed limbs. So one plan gives many tools, and a small change to one pair of limbs can open a new way of living. The hard skeleton also keeps water in, which let arthropods live on dry land. The price is that an arthropod must shed the skeleton to grow.
examples: A barnacle is an arthropod. The barnacle stands head down inside a shell and kicks food into the mouth with feathery legs.
A horseshoe crab, seen on the coast of Odisha, is a closer relative of spiders than of crabs.
A woodlouse under a flowerpot is a relative of crabs and prawns who lives on land.
explanations.art: A prawn seen from the side with each kind of limb drawn in a different colour: feelers, jaws, walking legs, paddles and tail fan.
explanations.definition: An arthropod is an animal with a hard outer skeleton, a body made of segments, and limbs that bend at joints.

explanations.concept: Echinoderms: five parts and feet that work by water power
explanations.description: Starfish, brittle stars, sea urchins, sand dollars, sea cucumbers and feather stars are echinoderms. About 7,000 kinds are alive today, and every one lives in the sea. No echinoderm lives in fresh water or on land. Their plan has two special features. The first is five matching parts around a centre. You can see five arms on a starfish and five bands of tube feet on a sea urchin's shell. The second is the water vascular system. Sea water enters through a small sieve plate on the body and fills a ring canal and five side canals. Each tube foot is joined to a small bulb. When muscles squeeze the bulb, water is pushed into the foot and the foot stretches out. A starfish has hundreds of tube feet and no brain. A ring of nerves runs round the mouth, and one nerve runs down each arm. The arm that is in front for the moment leads, and the others follow.
examples: A sea cucumber is an echinoderm lying on one side. The five bands run along the body.
In India, all sea cucumbers have been protected by law since 2001, and nobody may collect them.
A sea urchin's spines and tube feet both help in walking.
explanations.art: A starfish turned over to show rows of tube feet, with a zoom-in of one tube foot and the bulb that squeezes water into it.
explanations.definition: An echinoderm is a sea animal whose adult body is arranged in five matching parts, with chalky plates in the skin and many small tube feet worked by water pressure.

explanations.concept: A starfish is a closer relative of yours than a crab is
explanations.description: A starfish has no head, no backbone and five arms. A crab has eyes, legs and a brain. So which one is our closer relative? The starfish. Scientists worked this out in two ways. First, they watched eggs grow. A very young animal is a hollow ball of cells, and a dent forms in the ball. In a snail or an insect, the mouth forms at or near that first dent. In a starfish, a fish or a human, the first dent becomes the back end of the gut, and the mouth breaks through later in another place. This rule is simplified. Some animals do not follow it neatly, so by itself it could mislead. The second way settled the matter. Scientists compared the DNA of many animals, and the DNA puts echinoderms on the same branch as the animals with backbones. So 'invertebrate' is not one family. It is a name for many separate branches, and one of those branches is nearer to us than to the rest.
examples: A baby starfish has a left side and a right side, like you. The five-part body comes later.
The last ancestor shared by an octopus and a human lived more than 500 million years ago.
Insects and crabs are closer relatives of each other than either is of a snail.
explanations.art: A simple branching tree with sponges at the lowest branch, then cnidarians, then a fork: one side holding molluscs and arthropods, the other holding echinoderms and a child.
explanations.definition: Echinoderms and animals with backbones belong to the same large branch of the animal family tree. Molluscs and arthropods belong to another branch.

explanations.concept: Five ways to carry messages: none, a net, a ring, a chain of knots, and a brain with eight arm cords
explanations.description: A nerve cell is a long cell that passes a fast electrical signal to the next cell. The five phyla arrange their nerve cells very differently. A sponge has no nerve cells. Signals pass slowly from cell to cell as chemicals. A cnidarian has a nerve net spread through the body, with no centre. An echinoderm has a ring of nerves around the mouth and one nerve along each arm, with no brain. An arthropod has a brain in the head and a chain of ganglia along the body, one or more for each segment. Much of an insect's walking is run by the ganglia nearest the legs. A mollusc has several ganglia. In a snail these are small. In an octopus they have grown and joined into a large brain wrapped around the food pipe, and a thick nerve cord runs down each arm. So a brain in a head is one arrangement among several. Each arrangement fits a way of living: fixed in one place, drifting, creeping in any direction, or hunting.
examples: An ant's brain is smaller than a mustard seed, yet she finds her way home across a courtyard.
A jellyfish swims with steady beats, and no brain sets the beat. Small clusters of nerve cells around the rim of the bell set it.
Your own gut has a few hundred million nerve cells of its own. They run digestion with little help from your brain.
explanations.art: Five small body outlines in a row, a sponge, a jellyfish, a starfish, an ant and an octopus, each with the nerve cells drawn in red.
explanations.definition: A nervous system is all the nerve cells of an animal and the way they are joined. The five phyla in this unit arrange it in five ways.

explanations.concept: The octopus: a mollusc who gave up the shell
explanations.description: An octopus has all the mollusc parts, changed. Her mantle is the muscular bag behind the eyes that holds the hearts, the gills and the gut. Her foot has become eight arms and a funnel. She pulls water into the mantle and squirts it out through the funnel to shoot backwards. In her mouth are a hard beak like a parrot's and a radula. The ancestors of octopuses had shells, as the nautilus still has. Why would an animal give up a shell? A shell protects, but it is heavy and stiff. Without one, an octopus can squeeze through any gap wider than her beak, hunt in cracks, and change shape. The price is a soft body that any fish can bite. So she lives by hiding, by changing the colour and texture of her skin, by squirting ink, and by learning quickly. About 300 kinds of octopus are known. Many kinds live only a year or two. A mother guards her eggs without feeding, and dies around the time they hatch.
examples: In Vembar and other villages on the Gulf of Mannar coast of Tamil Nadu, fishers catch octopus on the reef beds.
A cuttlefish keeps a small shell inside the body. It is the white cuttlebone given to cage birds to peck.
A squid has eight arms and two longer tentacles. An octopus has eight arms and no tentacles.
explanations.art: An octopus drawn in side view with the mantle, funnel, eye, beak and arms labelled, and a small nautilus in a coiled shell beside her.
explanations.definition: An octopus is a cephalopod, a mollusc with eight arms around the mouth, no shell and a large brain.

explanations.description: Why three hearts? Blood picks up oxygen in the gills, where it must squeeze through a great many very fine tubes. Pushing through fine tubes slows a liquid down and uses up its pressure. In a fish, one heart pushes blood through the gills and the same push must then carry it round the whole body, so the blood reaches the body slowly. An octopus has a pump on each side of the problem. Blood coming back from the body enters the two gill hearts. Each one pushes it through a gill. The blood, now carrying oxygen, flows into the main heart, which gives it a fresh, strong push to the body. Your own heart does the same job with two halves: the right half pumps to the lungs and the left half pumps to the body. An octopus needs the strong push because her blood is a poor carrier. It carries oxygen with haemocyanin, which holds copper where our haemoglobin holds iron. The same amount of octopus blood carries several times less oxygen than human blood.
examples: Haemocyanin is blue when it carries oxygen and almost colourless when it does not.
In 1987, Martin Wells and his team measured the blood flow of swimming octopuses. The main heart stopped for a moment during each jet.
That is one reason an octopus mostly crawls. Fast swimming tires her quickly.
explanations.art: A simple loop diagram: body, two small hearts, two gills, one large heart, and back to the body, with the blood drawn pale before the gills and blue after them.
explanations.definition: An octopus has two gill hearts, each of which pushes blood through one gill, and one main heart, which pushes the blood from the gills around the body.

explanations.concept: Clever arms: most of an octopus's nerve cells are outside her brain
explanations.description: A human has about 86 billion nerve cells, and almost all of them are in the brain. An octopus is arranged differently. Each arm has a thick nerve cord down the middle, with a ganglion beside every sucker. An arm has no bones, so it can bend, twist, shorten or stiffen at any point. To steer such an arm from the brain alone, the brain would need to send a separate order to every part of it. Does the brain do that? In 2001, Germán Sumbre, Binyamin Hochner and their team tested arms whose nerve link to the brain had been cut. They gave the arm's nerve cord a small electrical signal. The arm reached out in a smooth wave, just as the arm of a whole octopus does. So the pattern for reaching is held in the arm's own nerve cord. The brain seems to send a short command, such as 'reach', and the arm works out the bends. Each sucker can also grip, let go and pass a small thing along to the next sucker.
examples: An octopus can search three cracks with three arms while her eyes watch something else.
Each arm carries hundreds of suckers, and each sucker can be moved by itself.
When you pull your hand off a hot tawa, the nerve cells in your backbone move the hand before your brain knows about the heat. That is a small human case of the same idea.
explanations.art: An octopus arm drawn large and cut away to show a cord down the middle with a small knot beside each sucker, and a much thinner line running back to the brain.
explanations.definition: A common octopus has about 500 million nerve cells. About two thirds of them are in the eight arms, in a nerve cord that runs down each arm.

explanations.description: An octopus hunts in holes where her eyes cannot see. So how does an arm know a crab from a stone? In 2020, Lena van Giesen and Nicholas Bellono's team at Harvard University studied the suckers of the California two-spot octopus. They found two kinds of sensing cell in the sucker skin. One kind senses touch and pressure. The other kind carries sensors for chemicals, including oily chemicals that do not spread well through water and so must be touched to be sensed. An arm that touches a crab senses the crab's chemicals and grips. An arm that touches a bare stone moves on. So a sucker does something like tasting and touching in one act. We do not know what that is like for the octopus. The suckers also tell her own body from other things. In 2014, Nir Nesher and his team found that suckers will not grip octopus skin, because a chemical in the skin stops them. That may be why eight arms rarely tangle.
examples: Dip a finger in sugar water and you learn that it is wet. You need your tongue to learn that it is sweet.
A fly tastes with her feet when she lands on food.
A catfish has taste buds over the whole skin.
explanations.art: An octopus arm inside a rock crack touching a small crab, with a zoom-in of one sucker showing two kinds of small cells in its skin.
explanations.definition: The skin of an octopus sucker has cells that sense touch and other cells that sense chemicals on whatever the sucker touches.

explanations.concept: Who is in charge, the brain or the arms?
explanations.description: An octopus's mind is at work in her arms as well as in her head. The nerve cells in an arm sense, weigh and act, and that is thinking. Scientists agree on the experiments and argue about what they mean. The arms do a great deal alone: the reaching pattern, the grip of each sucker and the sorting of food from stone. But the brain is not shut out. In 2011, Tamar Gutnick and her team gave octopuses a see-through maze with food in one of three boxes. The food was out of the water, so the arm could not sense its chemicals. The octopuses learned to steer one arm to the right box by watching it. In 2020, the same group showed that the brain can also learn from what a single arm feels. So the arms are not eight separate animals, and the brain is not a boss who orders every bend. The work is shared, and nobody yet knows exactly how.
examples: An octopus watching a crab chooses which arm to send. That choice is made with the eyes and the brain.
Once the arm is in a crack, the suckers and the arm's nerve cord do the searching.
Engineers who build soft robot arms copy this plan: a simple command from the centre, and the details worked out along the arm.

perspectives.who: Binyamin Hochner and his team at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem
perspectives.explanation: The octopus's body, arms and brain form one working whole. Much of the control of movement is handed to the arms. The brain does not even seem to keep a detailed map of where each arm is.
The arms can act alone, but the brain also directs them and learns from them. In the maze tests, the learning happened in the brain. So the arms do not have minds wholly of their own.

perspectives.who: Sidney Carls-Diamante, a philosopher, writing in 2017
perspectives.explanation: If so much sensing and deciding happens in each arm, an octopus might not have one single stream of experience as a human seems to have. She might have several that work together. Nobody knows how to test this yet.

explanations.art: An octopus with one arm in a clear plastic maze, her eye turned towards the arm, and three other arms each busy with something else.

explanations.concept: Where animals came from: single cells who stayed together
explanations.description: Go back far enough and the ancestors of every animal were single cells living in water. How did single cells become bodies? A clue lives in ponds and seas today. Choanoflagellates are single-celled living beings, and each one has a whip-like thread inside a collar of tiny fingers. They look almost exactly like the collar cells of a sponge. Their DNA shows that they are the closest living relatives of all animals. Some kinds can also divide and stay stuck together as a small ball of cells. Nicole King and her team in California found in 2012 that one kind forms these balls when the cells sense a chemical made by a certain bacterium. So the first step towards an animal body may have been cells that divided and did not let go. Later steps gave the cells different jobs. This is a well-supported idea, but nobody watched it happen, and the details are still argued over.
examples: Every animal body, including yours, starts as one cell that divides and whose cells stay together.
A sponge's collar cell and a free-living choanoflagellate are hard to tell apart under a microscope.
You are made of about 30 trillion cells that all came from one fertilised egg.

perspectives.who: Nicole King and many other biologists
perspectives.explanation: Animals arose from single cells like choanoflagellates that stayed together after dividing. The likeness between collar cells and choanoflagellates is inherited from that shared ancestor.

perspectives.who: Some biologists who study sponge cells closely
perspectives.explanation: The likeness may be only skin deep. A 2019 study led by Shunsuke Sogabe found that the genes switched on in sponge collar cells are not especially like those of choanoflagellates. The first animal cells may have been cells that could change freely from one type to another.

explanations.art: A single cell with a collar and a thread on the left, a small ball of the same cells in the middle, and a sponge wall lined with collar cells on the right.

agreed.text: Sponges are animals, although they have no mouth, muscles or nerve cells.
agreed.evidence: Robert Grant watched living sponges pump water in 1825. Their cells have no cell walls, they eat other living things, and their DNA places them on the animal family tree.

agreed.text: The reaching movement of an octopus arm is worked out in the arm's own nerve cord.
agreed.evidence: In 2001, Sumbre, Hochner and their team gave a small signal to the nerve cord of arms no longer linked to the brain. The arms reached out with the same wave as in a whole octopus.

agreed.text: An octopus has three hearts: two that push blood through the gills and one that pushes it round the body.
agreed.evidence: The hearts can be seen when an octopus is opened up, and pressure measurements in living octopuses by Martin Wells's team in the 1980s showed what each heart does.

agreed.text: A stinging cell fires in less than a millionth of a second.
agreed.evidence: In 2006, Timm Nüchter's team filmed hydra stinging cells at more than a million pictures a second. The fastest part took about 700 billionths of a second.

agreed.text: Echinoderms are closer relatives of animals with backbones than of molluscs or arthropods.
agreed.evidence: The early growth of the egg is alike in starfish and in animals with backbones, and comparisons of DNA from many animals give the same answer.

agreed.text: Arthropods have more named kinds than all other animals together.
agreed.evidence: Lists of named species kept by museums and universities hold more than a million arthropods, most of them insects.

challenging.claim: Sponges are plants, or something between a plant and an animal.
challenging.who: Many naturalists before 1825, including Carl Linnaeus in his early lists.
challenging.for: A sponge is fixed to one spot, has branches, and does not flinch quickly when touched.
challenging.against: Robert Grant saw living sponges pump water. Sponges eat bacteria, have no cell walls and make sperm and eggs.
challenging.context: This was the usual view of sponges for about two thousand years.

challenging.claim: Each octopus arm has a mind of its own, so an octopus has nine brains.
challenging.for: Two thirds of the nerve cells are in the arms. An arm cut off from the brain can still reach and grip.
challenging.against: The brain chooses which arm to send and where, and learns from what one arm feels, as Tamar Gutnick's maze tests showed in 2011 and 2020. An arm's nerve cord is not built like a brain.
challenging.context: 'Nine brains' is a catchy line. Scientists who study octopus arms do not use it.

challenging.claim: Comb jellies, not sponges, are the oldest branch of the animal family tree.
challenging.who: Darrin Schultz and his team in 2023, and others before them.
challenging.for: The order of genes along the chromosomes of comb jellies matches single-celled relatives of animals, while sponges share a rearranged order with all other animals.
challenging.against: Sponges have no nerve cells or muscles, which fits a very early branch. Some DNA studies still put sponges first.
challenging.context: If comb jellies branched first, then nerve cells either arose twice or were lost in sponges.

challenging.claim: An animal needs a brain to learn.
challenging.for: The animals we see learning tricks, such as dogs and parrots, all have large brains.
challenging.against: Box jellyfish have no brain. In 2023, Jan Bielecki and his team showed that they learn to steer around obstacles after a few bumps.
challenging.context: The box jellyfish has only small clusters of nerve cells beside the eyes.

challenging.claim: Invertebrates are simple animals, and animals with backbones are the advanced ones.
challenging.who: An old habit in textbooks, going back to the ladder of life drawn by Aristotle's followers.
challenging.for: Animals with backbones include the largest animals and those with the largest brains.
challenging.against: Every living animal has ancestors as old as ours. An octopus's eye, a bee's dance and a coral reef are not simple. 'Invertebrate' names many branches that are no closer to each other than to us.
challenging.context: The word 'invertebrate' was coined by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck around 1800.

big_questions.q: In the Boss or Hand test, who found the coin: the boss, the hand, or both together?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one knew that the other did not.

big_questions.q: If an octopus arm senses a crab and grips, and the brain never ordered it, who decided?
big_questions.hint: Is 'the octopus' her brain, her arms, or all of her?

big_questions.q: A sponge pressed through cloth becomes loose cells, and the cells build a sponge again. Was the sponge one animal or many?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the cells did when they were alone, and what they did together.

big_questions.q: A coral colony is thousands of polyps who share food. A reef is thousands of colonies. Where does one living being stop and the next begin?
big_questions.hint: There may be more than one good answer.

big_questions.q: Your gut has hundreds of millions of nerve cells that work without asking your brain. Is that part of you thinking?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to know to answer?

big_questions.q: Why do we give a name, 'invertebrates', to a group that is only joined by what its members lack?
big_questions.hint: Who made the list, and what were they comparing the animals with?

big_questions.q: An octopus lives one or two years and learns everything alone, with no parent to teach her. What does that say about learning?
big_questions.hint: Compare with how much of what you know came from other people.

story.title: The Net with Eight Hands
story.note: A made-up story. Thangam, her grandmother and her cousins are imagined. Vembar is a real fishing village on the Gulf of Mannar coast of Tamil Nadu, where fishers catch octopus on the reef beds, and where the octopus is called pei kanava. Nets with floats along the top rope are real, and so is the way an octopus searches several cracks at once with different arms while her eyes watch something else.
text: The storm tide brought the net back in the night. In the morning it lay along the sand at Vembar like a thick grey rope, longer than six boats. It was rolled up with weed, crab shells, sticks, half a palm leaf and somebody's slipper.
Paatti looked at it with her hands on her hips. 'The boat goes out at four,' she said. 'By then this net must be clean and folded. Thangam, you are the eldest. You are in charge.'
Thangam was ten. There were eight of them that morning, counting her, and the smallest was Mari, who was five. Thangam climbed onto an upturned basket so that she could see the whole net.
'Nobody touch anything until I say,' she said. 'Selvam, lift that bit by the red float. No, the next float. Wait. Kani, pull the weed out from under his hand. Not yet! He hasn't lifted it.'
Selvam lifted. Kani pulled. The weed came out, and a knot behind it pulled tight, because Kani could not see the knot and Thangam could not see it either, from the basket.
'Stop,' said Thangam. 'Everybody stop.'
Everybody had already stopped. Six children were standing with their arms hanging, waiting to be told what to do. Mari had sat down and was burying her own feet.
Thangam got down and looked at the knot. Then she got up on the basket again. 'Deepa, hold the top rope. Higher. Arul, find the end of that stick. No, the other end.'
'Which other end?' said Arul. 'It has two.'

By the time the sun was above the casuarina trees, they had cleared the net from the first float to the fourth. Thangam counted the floats that were left. There were more than sixty. Her throat was sore from shouting, and her head was full of other people's hands.
'Drink some water,' she said. 'I'm going to wash.'
She walked down to where the flat rocks began. The tide had left pools in them, warm at the edges. She crouched by the largest one and put her hands in.
Something in the pool was looking at her.

It took her a moment to find the eye. It sat in a lump the colour of the rock, under a ledge, and it had a dark bar across it like a slit in a door. A pei kanava. A small one, no bigger than Thangam's two fists. The fishers brought big ones home in baskets, but she had never watched a live one this close.

The octopus did not move, and her eye did not leave Thangam. But she was busy all the same. One arm was stretched across the floor of the pool and had gone into a crack up to its thick part. Another arm was under a stone on the far side. A third was feeling along the edge of an old oyster shell, sucker by sucker, the way Paatti's fingers went along a hem.
The eye stayed on Thangam the whole time.

The arm in the crack went still. Then it began to come out, slowly, and something came with it: a crab the size of a one-rupee coin, held by two suckers. The suckers passed the crab along to the next two, and those passed the crab on again, like buckets going down a line of people at a fire. The crab went under the web of skin between the arms and was gone.

And still the eye watched Thangam. The octopus had not looked at the crack once. She could not have seen into it anyway. The arm under the stone was still searching. The arm at the oyster shell had moved on to a clump of weed.
Thangam stayed very still, with her hands in the warm water. Nobody was telling that arm which way to bend, she thought. It was in the crack. It could feel the crab. The eye could not.
She looked back up the beach. Seven children stood by the net with their arms hanging down, and every one of them was looking at the basket where she had been standing.
She walked back fast.

'Listen,' she said, and she did not climb on the basket. 'Everybody take a piece of net, from one float to the next float. That piece is yours. Start at your float and work along. Feel for the knots with your fingers before you pull anything. You can feel what I can't see.'
'What if there's a stick?' said Arul.
'Then take the stick out.'
'What if it's stuck?'
'Then shout, and I'll come.'
'What do I do?' said Mari.
'You carry the weed to the pile. All of it. That's your job, and nobody else's.'

For a while nobody spoke. Thangam walked along the net from one end to the other, and this time she looked at the whole of it. Where the weed was thick she moved Selvam and Deepa to work next to each other. Where a piece was clean already she sent Kani four floats further down. Twice somebody shouted, and twice she went, and once it took three of them to work a palm stalk out of the mesh.
Mostly she had nothing to say. That felt strange. Eight pairs of hands were working, and seven of them were doing things she could not see and had not ordered.
When the shadow of the boat reached the water, the net lay in a clean folded heap as high as Mari's chest.
Paatti came down the beach at half past three and walked round the heap. She pulled out an arm's length of mesh and ran it through her fingers, and found nothing to pick out.
'I heard you shouting all morning,' she said. 'Then I didn't hear you at all. I thought you had all run off. Who taught you to stop shouting?'
'A pei kanava,' said Thangam. 'In the rock pool.'
Paatti looked at her for a while. 'And what did she charge for the lesson?'
'One crab,' said Thangam. 'She had already taken it.'
story.epiphany: The octopus's eye chose where to keep watch, and each arm worked out its own crack by touch. Thangam ran the net the same way. She kept the whole net in view and said where people were needed, and each pair of hands found its own knots.
ask: Why could the arm in the crack find the crab when the eye could not?
What did the octopus's eye do that her arms could not do?
What kinds of work go faster when one person gives every order? What kinds go slower?
How might an animal with no bones in her arms tell where each arm is?
Think of something your hands do well without your eyes. How did they learn it?

roots.context: In the Boss or Hand test you compared ordering every move with giving only the aim. You also met a sponge with no nerve cells, a starfish with no brain, and an octopus with most of her nerve cells in her arms. Now we ask what this tells us about where deciding happens, in them and in you.

deep_truth.truth: In the Boss or Hand test, giving an order for every small move was slow. The coin came up sooner when the boss gave only the aim and the hand worked out the rest by touch. An octopus shares the work this way too. About two thirds of her nerve cells are in her arms, and each arm works out its own bends. So in an octopus, deciding is spread through the body, and much of it happens where the touching happens.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the brain' for the place where an animal decides, as if every body were run from one control room in the head. That fits a human fairly well, so we treat it as the rule. Then an animal with no brain, or with most of her nerve cells in her arms, looks like a lesser animal, when she is only arranged differently.
deep_truth.evidence: In 2001, octopus arms with the link to the brain cut still reached out in the normal wave when the arm's nerve cord was given a signal. A sucker tells crab from stone by touch. A starfish walks with hundreds of tube feet and no brain. A sponge with no nerve cells squeezes the whole body to clear dirt.

three.who_am_i: You are also run from more than one place. Your backbone's nerve cells pull your hand off a hot tawa, and your gut's nerve cells run your digestion, and neither waits for your brain.
three.what_is_life: Every living body has to sense and act. A sponge does it with chemicals passed from cell to cell, a starfish with a ring of nerves, an octopus with a brain and eight arm cords.
three.what_is_this_world: The world an arm meets in a dark crack is made of touches and tastes. The world an eye meets is made of light. One octopus lives in both at once.

roots.thread: Every animal began as single cells that divided and stayed together. In a sponge, those cells still sense and answer each other with no nerve cells at all. In a jellyfish the sensing runs through a net, in a starfish through a ring, and in an octopus through a brain and eight arm cords. These are five arrangements of one activity, which is sensing and answering. That activity was there in the single cells before any body was built, and it is there in every part of a body now. A brain gathers a great deal of it into one place, and the rest of it goes on in the arms, the gut and the skin.

teachings.teaching: A student asks: sent by whom does the mind go out to what it thinks about? Who sets the first breath moving? Who directs the eye and the ear?
teachings.link: The student is asking who the boss is, and the Upanishad does not point to any one part of the body. The octopus puts the same question to science: when an arm grips a crab that the brain never saw, who sent the arm?

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 3, the story of Cook Ding (paraphrased)
teachings.teaching: A cook who has cut up oxen for nineteen years says that he no longer looks with his eyes. His knowing and planning stop, and his hands follow the natural gaps in the ox.
teachings.link: The cook describes skill that lives in the hands and works best when the planning mind stops giving orders. In the Boss or Hand test, your hand found the coin sooner when it was left to feel its own way.
verse: 今臣之刀，十九年矣，所解數千牛矣，而刀刃若新發於硎。
彼節者有間，而刀刃者无厚，以无厚入有間，恢恢乎其於遊刃必有餘地矣

teachings.source: Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda), Book 2, chapter 1, the chariot (paraphrased)
teachings.teaching: The monk Nagasena asks the king whether the chariot is the axle, the wheels, the frame or the pole. It is none of them alone. 'Chariot' is a name for the parts working together.
teachings.link: Is the octopus her brain, or her arms? Nagasena's answer would be that 'octopus' names all of them working together. Scientists who study her arms say something close to this.

science.text: The pattern for an octopus arm's reach is held in the arm's own nerve cord, not sent bend by bend from the brain.
How the brain and the arms share decisions, and how much the brain knows about what each arm is doing, is still being worked out.
Some philosophers ask whether an octopus has one stream of experience or several. Nobody has found a way to test this.

other_view.who: Tamar Gutnick and Michael Kuba, who test how octopuses learn, and most scientists who study brains
other_view.view: They agree that an octopus arm can run movements alone. But they point out that our spinal cord does that too, and we do not say that our spinal cord thinks. In their maze tests the learning happened in the octopus's central brain, which then guided the arm. On this view the arms carry out skilled routines, and deciding and experience still belong to the brain. It is a careful view, held by people who know these animals well.

practice.title: Let the hands find it
practice.say: Sit down and close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Now, with your eyes still closed, tie a loose knot in a handkerchief, or do up a button. Go slowly. Notice your fingers finding their way. Notice that you did not tell each finger what to do. Now rest your hands in your lap. Feel your breath going in and out by itself. Ask yourself quietly how much of you is working right now without being told.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Tie a loose knot in a hanky. Notice your fingers finding the way. Did you tell each finger what to do? Now rest. What else in you is working without being told?

ask: When your fingers do up a button with your eyes shut, who knows how to do it: you, or your fingers?
If most of an octopus's nerve cells are in her arms, where is the octopus?
A sponge has no nerve cells and still acts as one body. What do you think holds a body together as one?
roots.art: A child sitting with closed eyes, tying a knot in a handkerchief, and beside her in a bowl of sea water a small octopus with one arm curled round a shell.

printables.title: The clue sheet: five groups and how to know them
items: SPONGE: a body full of pores. No mouth, no gut, no nerve cells. Fixed to one spot.
CNIDARIAN: a soft body with one opening, ringed by tentacles with stinging cells.
MOLLUSC: a soft body with no segments, covered by a mantle. Most have a foot and a shell.
ARTHROPOD: a hard outer skeleton, a body in segments, and legs that bend at joints.
ECHINODERM: a body in five matching parts, with tube feet. Lives only in the sea.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Beans for a true body clue

rules: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them and put them in one pile with the animal names facing up. Put a bowl of about 80 dry beans in the middle. Keep the clue sheet where everyone can read it.
On your turn, read the name on the top card. Do not turn the card over yet.
Say which of the five groups the animal belongs to. Then say one body clue for that group, such as 'jointed legs' or 'tube feet'.
Turn the card over. If your group is right, take 1 bean. If your clue is true for that group, take 1 more bean. Any true clue from the clue sheet counts.
If the back says TRAP CARD, take double beans for whatever you got right.
If your group is wrong, take no beans. Read the back aloud so that everyone hears the right group and the clue.
Put the used card aside. The next player takes a turn. The game ends when the pile is finished, and the player with the most beans wins.
Playing alone: go through all 30 cards. The most you can get is 76 beans. Try to beat 50.
