flow.do: Cut out and shuffle the cards. Pile them name side up. Read the five lines of the clue sheet aloud together. Ask your child to say each group's clue back in their own words.
flow.say: Here are five groups of animals without backbones. Let us read how to know each one. Now tell me each clue in your own words.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Read the clue sheet. Say each group's clue in your own words.
flow.context: This is the first step of Group Detective. You set up the cards and learn the five clues.
flow.parent: If you have no printer, write the 30 names on slips of paper and keep this list of answers beside you. Dry beans can choke a child under five, so keep them out of reach of very young children.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. Each player says the group and one body clue. Then they turn the card over and take 1 bean for the right group and 1 for a right clue. A trap card pays double. Read the back aloud whenever the group was wrong.
flow.say: Read the card. Which group, and what is your clue? Now turn it over and see.
flow.kid: Read the top card. Say the group and a clue. Turn it over and take your beans.
flow.context: In this step of Group Detective you play the first ten cards.

ask.q: What do you look for first when you decide on a group?
good: Whether the body is hard or soft.
Whether it has legs with joints.
Whether it has five parts or tube feet.

flow.parent: Accept any true clue from the clue sheet. If your child gives a clue that is true of the animal but not of the whole group, such as 'lives in the sea', ask for a clue about the body.

flow.do: Play the other twenty cards. When a trap card comes up, stop after it is turned over. Ask what made the animal look like a member of another group.
flow.say: That was a trap card. What did this animal look like? Which body clue shows the real group?
flow.kid: Play the rest of the cards. On a trap card, say what fooled you.
flow.context: In this step of Group Detective you finish the pile and look closely at the trap cards.

check.q: A barnacle is stuck to a rock inside a hard shell. Why is the barnacle an arthropod and not a mollusc?
options: The animal inside has jointed legs
check.why: Groups are decided by the body plan, and a barnacle has jointed legs and sheds a skeleton, as crabs do. If you picked the shell, remember that a hard cover can be built by very different animals. Molluscs and arthropods both live in the sea, so the home does not settle the question.

flow.parent: The eight traps are the bluebottle, sea fan, cuttlefish, barnacle, horseshoe crab, woodlouse, sea cucumber and feather star. Most players miss several the first time, and that is the point of them.

flow.do: Count the beans. Ask your child which group was easiest to spot and which was hardest, and why.
flow.say: Count your beans. Which group was easiest to spot? Which was hardest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count your beans. Which group was easiest? Which was hardest? Say why.
flow.context: This is the last step of Group Detective. You count up and say which groups were hard to spot.
flow.think: Why do you think so many sea animals who stay in one place look like plants?

experiments.title: Boss or Hand? The blind reach test
experiments.context: In this test one person keeps their eyes shut and uses one hand to find a coin hidden among chana on a big plate. Another person can see. You try three ways of sharing the work between the one who sees and the hand that feels, and time each way. You will find out whether orders from the eyes help the hand or slow it down.
experiments.question: A hand has to find a coin among chana without looking. Which is quickest: a boss who can see ordering every move, the hand searching alone by touch, or the boss giving only the aim and the hand doing the rest?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Which of the three ways will find the coin in the shortest time, and which will take longest? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same person is the hand in every try, and uses the same hand. The plate, the coin and the number of chana stay the same. The boss moves the coin to a new place before every try, while the hand's eyes are shut, so that remembering does not help. Each try starts with the fingers on the near edge of the plate. You do three rounds, and in each round the three ways come in a different order. That way, no one way gets all the benefit of practice. No try goes past 60 seconds.

materials.item: a big steel plate or tray, the bigger the better
chana, groundnuts or other dry beans
a dupatta or towel to cover the eyes, or simply shut them
a timer, such as the stopwatch on a phone
the results table, drawn on paper, and a pencil

experiments.safety: Dry beans and coins can choke a child under five, so keep them out of reach of very young children.

schedule.what: Guess, do three rounds of three tries, swap places for two tries, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Write the seconds for every try, and the number of orders in each Way 1 try. Add up the three times for each way. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Example: total seconds for three tries, one family
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what a chart of results looks like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: A large steel plate on a table with about thirty chana spread over it and one coin among them, a phone showing a stopwatch beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Spread 30 chana on a big plate. Hide one coin among them.

setup.art: A child with a dupatta over her eyes, one hand resting on the near edge of the plate, and a parent sitting opposite pointing and speaking.
setup.caption: 2. Way 1: the boss orders every move. The hand does only what it is told.

setup.art: The same child searching the plate with her fingertips while the parent sits silent with a hand over her own mouth.
setup.caption: 3. Way 2: the boss says nothing. The hand searches by touch.

setup.art: The parent saying one sentence with a speech bubble reading 'far edge, on your left', and the child's hand moving straight towards that part of the plate.
setup.caption: 4. Way 3: the boss says where to aim, once. The hand does the rest.

flow.do: Read the question aloud and explain the three ways. Ask your child which way will be quickest and which slowest, and why. Write the guesses above the table. Do not say whether you agree.
flow.say: One of us will be the hand, with eyes shut. The other will be the boss, who can see. We will try three ways. In Way 1, the boss orders every move. In Way 2, the boss says nothing. In Way 3, the boss says where to aim, once. Which will find the coin soonest? Which will be slowest? Why?
flow.kid: Which way will find the coin soonest? Which will be slowest? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Boss or Hand test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: What can the boss do that the hand cannot? What can the hand do that the boss cannot?
good: The boss can see where the coin is.
The hand can feel the coin and the chana.
The boss does not know when the fingers touch something.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children are sure that the boss who can see will be quickest.

flow.do: Make the results table on paper. Spread the chana on the plate. Agree on the eight orders the boss may use in Way 1: left, right, forward, back, down, pinch, lift and stop. Practise them once with eyes open.
flow.say: In Way 1, I may say only these words: left, right, forward, back, down, pinch, lift, stop. You do exactly what I say, and nothing else.
flow.kid: Learn the eight orders: left, right, forward, back, down, pinch, lift, stop.
flow.context: In this step you get the Boss or Hand test ready and learn the eight orders.
flow.parent: Your child is the hand for all nine tries. The honest rule for Way 1 matters most. The hand must wait for an order even when the fingers can feel the coin. Explain that this is what we are testing.

flow.do: Round 1. Your child shuts their eyes and rests their fingers on the near edge. Move the coin. Do Way 1 and count your orders. Move the coin and do Way 2 in silence. Move the coin and do Way 3 with one sentence. Time each try and write it down.
flow.say: Eyes shut, fingers on the edge. First I order every move. Next you search alone. Last I tell you once where to aim.
flow.kid: Eyes shut. Fingers on the edge. Try all three ways. Wait for the word 'go'.
flow.context: In this step you do round 1 of the Boss or Hand test, with the three ways in order 1, 2, 3.
flow.parent: Stop the timer when the coin is lifted clear of the plate. If a try reaches 60 seconds, stop and write '60, stopped'. In Way 3, say only one sentence, such as 'It is near the far edge, on your left', and then stay silent. A coin lying flat on steel is hard to pinch, and sliding it to the rim is allowed in every way.

flow.do: Round 2 uses the order Way 2, Way 3, Way 1. Round 3 uses the order Way 3, Way 1, Way 2. Move the coin before every try. Time each try, count the orders in Way 1, and write everything down.
flow.say: Round 2 starts with the hand alone. Round 3 starts with the aim only. I will move the coin each time.
flow.kid: Do rounds 2 and 3. The order of the ways changes each round.
flow.context: In this step you do rounds 2 and 3 of the Boss or Hand test, changing the order of the ways.

check.q: Why do the three ways come in a different order in each round?
options: So practice does not help only one way
So the game is less boring
So the coin is harder to find
check.why: The hand gets better with practice. If Way 3 always came last, it would get the most practice and might win for that reason alone. Changing the order shares the practice out. If you picked 'harder to find', remember that moving the coin does that job, and the order of the ways does something different.

flow.parent: Hide the coin in a new part of the plate each time: near, far, left, right and middle. Do not make it easier or harder for any one way.

flow.do: Swap places for two tries. Your child is now the boss and you are the hand. Do Way 1 once and Way 3 once. Then ask your child what it was like to give every order.
flow.say: Now you are the boss and I am the hand. Order every move first. Then give me only the aim. Which was harder for you?
flow.kid: Now you are the boss. Order every move. Then give only the aim. Which was harder?
flow.context: In this step of the Boss or Hand test you swap places, so that your child finds out what the boss's job is like.

ask.q: What was hard about ordering every move?
good: I had to think of every small step.
I did not know what your fingers were touching.
My words were too slow for your hand.

flow.parent: These two tries are not written in the table. They let your child feel how much the boss has to do in Way 1.

flow.do: Add up the three times for each way. Ask your child which way was quickest and slowest, and what the count of orders shows. They write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Give the explanation in the parent note only after they have finished.
flow.say: Add up the times. Which way was quickest? Which was slowest? How many orders did Way 1 need? Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Add up the times. Which way won? Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the Boss or Hand test show.

ask.q: Why was ordering every move slow?
good: Each order takes time to say and to obey.
The boss did not know what the fingers were touching.
It took many orders to do one small thing.

ask.q: An octopus arm has no bones and can bend anywhere along it. What would happen if her brain had to order every bend of eight arms?
good: It would be far too slow.
The brain would have too many orders to give.
It would be better if each arm worked out its own bends.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. The boss can see the whole plate but is not touching it. The hand is touching it but has no view of it. Way 1 uses only the boss's knowledge and pays for it with many slow orders. Way 3 uses both. An octopus works more like Way 3. Her eyes and brain choose where to send an arm, and the arm's own nerve cord works out the bending, while the suckers tell food from stone. Be honest about the limits of the model. Your child's hand is not an octopus arm, and its moves were still worked out in your child's own brain and backbone. The test shows only why sharing the work is quicker. If Way 2 beat Way 3 on your plate, the plate was small enough to search quickly without help. Say so, and ask what would happen on a plate the size of a room.
flow.think: Your eyes were shut, yet your fingers knew a coin from a chana at once. How did they know?

experiments.title: Sea Soup: what can a filter catch?
experiments.context: In this test you mix a 'sea soup' of tea leaves, turmeric powder and a little milk in water. You pour it through a tea strainer, then one layer of cloth, then four layers of cloth, and look at what each filter stops. A sponge feeds by filtering, so this shows what a filter can and cannot do. You will find out which bits a filter catches and which slip through.
experiments.question: Tea leaves, turmeric powder and milk are mixed in water. Which of them will a tea strainer stop? Which will one layer of cotton cloth stop? Which will four layers stop?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. For each of the three filters, say which things will be stopped and which will pass through. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: All three filters get the same soup, one after another, so each filter is tested on whatever passed the filter before. You pour slowly each time, without pressing or squeezing the cloth. You look at every tumbler in the same light, standing on the same printed page.
results_table: Colour of the water that passed
Can you read print through it? (yes, just, no)

materials.item: a clean white cotton handkerchief or a piece of old cotton cloth, which will be stained yellow

schedule.what: Guess, mix the soup, pour it through three filters, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each filter. Under the table write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

setup.art: A tumbler of water with tea leaves floating in it, a spoon of yellow powder being tipped in, and a small spoon of milk beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Stir a pinch of tea leaves, a quarter teaspoon of turmeric and a teaspoon of milk into a tumbler of water.

setup.art: A child pouring the cloudy yellow mixture through a tea strainer held over a second tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the soup through a tea strainer into the next tumbler. Look at what stayed behind.

setup.art: A white cotton cloth stretched over the mouth of a third tumbler with a yellow patch forming as liquid is poured through.
setup.caption: 3. Pour it through one layer of cotton cloth. Then through the cloth folded into four layers.

setup.art: Four tumblers in a row standing on a newspaper, from cloudy with leaves to pale and cloudy, with a child looking down through each at the print.
setup.caption: 4. Stand each tumbler on a newspaper. Look down through the water. Can you read the print?

flow.do: Show your child the tea leaves, the turmeric, the milk and the three filters. Ask what each filter will stop and what will pass, and why. Write the guesses down. Do not say whether you agree.
flow.say: We will mix these three things into water and pour the mixture through three filters. What will each filter stop? What will get through? Why?
flow.kid: What will each filter stop? What will get through? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sea Soup test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: What decides whether a thing passes through a filter?
good: Whether it is smaller than the holes.
How big the bits are.
How fine the cloth is.

flow.parent: Many children expect four layers of cloth to stop everything, including the milk. Let the guess stand.

flow.do: Stir the tea leaves, turmeric and milk into a tumbler of water. Keep one spoonful aside in a small bowl to compare later. Stand the tumbler on the newspaper and look down through it.
flow.say: Stir it well. This is our sea soup. Look down through it at the newspaper. Can you read anything?
flow.kid: Stir the soup. Stand it on the newspaper. Can you read the print through it?
flow.context: In this step of the Sea Soup test you mix the soup and look at it before filtering.
flow.parent: Turmeric stains cloth, fingers and some table tops. Work on a tray or an old newspaper.

flow.do: Hold the strainer over the second tumbler and pour the soup through slowly. Look at what stayed in the strainer and at the water that passed. Fill in the first row of the table.
flow.say: Pour slowly through the strainer. What stayed behind? What does the water look like now?
flow.kid: Pour the soup through the strainer. What stayed behind? Write it down.
flow.context: In this step of the Sea Soup test you use the first filter, a tea strainer.
flow.parent: The tea leaves stay in the strainer. The water stays yellow and cloudy, because the turmeric grains and the milk are much smaller than the holes.

flow.do: Stretch one layer of cloth over the third tumbler and pour the soup through slowly. Look at the cloth and the water, and fill in the row. Do not rinse the cloth. Fold a clean part of the cloth into four layers, pour through into the fourth tumbler, and fill in the last row.
flow.say: Now one layer of cloth. Pour slowly and watch the cloth. Now four layers. Is this slower? What is on the cloth?
flow.kid: Pour through one layer of cloth. Then through four layers. Watch the cloth each time.
flow.context: In this step of the Sea Soup test you use one layer of cloth and then four layers.

check.q: The soup drips more slowly through four layers of cloth than through one. Why?
options: The path is longer, narrower and partly blocked
The milk is holding it back
check.why: Four layers make smaller, longer gaps, and the turmeric caught in them blocks them further. A finer filter is always slower and clogs sooner. If you picked 'thicker', notice that the water is the same water. Only the path changed.

flow.parent: The cloth catches a yellow patch of turmeric, and four layers catch more. The water that passes is paler but still cloudy and a little yellow. The cloudiness is the milk, which gets through every time. If your cloth is very thin, fold it once for the 'one layer' pour.

flow.do: Stand all four tumblers on the newspaper and compare them. Ask your child what each filter stopped and what nothing stopped. They write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Give the explanation in the parent note only after they have finished.
flow.say: Look at all four. What did each filter stop? What got through every filter? Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: What did each filter stop? What got through them all? Write what you think, saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the Sea Soup test show.

ask.q: The milk passed every filter. What does that tell you about the bits in milk?
good: They are smaller than the gaps in the cloth.
They are too small to see one by one.

ask.q: A sponge feeds on bacteria, which are about as small as the droplets in milk. What kind of filter would the sponge need?
good: One with gaps much finer than cloth.
A very fine one, and a way to keep it from clogging.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. A filter stops only what is bigger than its gaps. Milk is cloudy because of droplets of fat and grains of protein, and the droplets are a few thousandths of a millimetre across. Bacteria are about that size as well. A sponge's collar cells have a ring of tiny fingers, and the gaps between the fingers are far smaller than the gaps in any cloth, so they catch what passed all your filters. The fine filter also clogs, as your cloth did. A sponge clears the dirt with slime and a slow squeeze.
flow.think: Your four-layer filter was slow and clogged. A sponge filters all day for years. What would a sponge need that your cloth does not have?

experiments.title: The Slow Sieve: why does an octopus have a heart at each gill?
experiments.context: In this test you time how long a tumbler of water takes to run through a funnel when the neck is empty, loosely packed with cotton and firmly packed with cotton. The packed cotton stands for the very fine tubes of a gill. Then you walk the path that blood takes through an octopus's three hearts. You will find out why an octopus needs an extra heart at each gill.
experiments.question: How much longer does a tumbler of water take to pass through a funnel when the neck is packed loosely with cotton, and when it is packed firmly?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Will the water take twice as long through loose cotton, five times as long, or more? What about firm cotton? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The funnel and the tumbler are the same for all three pours. You pour the same amount of water each time, and pour it all in at once. You start the timer when the water goes in and stop it when the stream turns to single drops. Only the packing in the neck changes.
results_table: Seconds for one tumbler to pass
How many times as long as the empty neck

materials.item: a funnel, or the top third of a plastic bottle cut off and turned upside down
cotton wool, or a wad of clean cotton cloth
materials.qty: a piece the size of a lemon

materials.item: a steel tumbler of water, the same amount each time
a bowl or bucket to catch the water
a timer, such as the stopwatch on a phone
three chairs or cushions, for the walk at the end

experiments.safety: If you make the funnel from a bottle, a grown-up does the cutting, and covers the cut edge with tape.

schedule.what: Guess, time three pours, then walk the path of the blood through three hearts.

experiments.record: Write the seconds for each pour. Work out how many times as long each packed pour took. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

setup.art: The top of a plastic bottle turned upside down as a funnel over a bowl, with a tumbler of water and a ball of cotton wool beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Set a funnel over a bowl. Have cotton and three tumblers of water ready.

setup.art: A child pouring a tumbler of water into the empty funnel while a parent holds a phone showing a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Pour one tumbler through the empty neck. Time it.

setup.art: The same funnel with a plug of cotton in its neck and water dripping slowly from it into the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Pack the neck loosely with cotton and time a pour. Then pack it firmly and time again.

setup.art: Three chairs in a triangle on the floor, two labelled 'gill heart' and one labelled 'main heart', with a child walking from one to the next.
setup.caption: 4. Walk the blood's path: body, gill heart, gill, main heart, body.

flow.do: Show the funnel and the cotton. Say that the cotton stands for the very fine tubes inside a gill. Ask your child how much longer the water will take through loose cotton and through firm cotton, and why. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Blood in a gill has to pass through very fine tubes. This cotton stands for them. How much longer will water take to get through it? Why?
flow.kid: How much longer will water take through cotton? Twice as long? More? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Slow Sieve test. You guess before you test.
flow.parent: If you are cutting a bottle to make the funnel, do it before you start, and tape the cut edge.

flow.do: Pour one tumbler through the empty funnel and time it. Push a loose plug of cotton into the neck, pour and time. Take the cotton out, push it back firmly, pour and time. Write each time down.
flow.say: First the empty neck. Now loose cotton. Now firm cotton. Start the timer as the water goes in. Stop when it only drips.
flow.kid: Time three pours: empty neck, loose cotton, firm cotton. Write each time down.
flow.context: In this step of the Slow Sieve test you time water passing through an empty neck, loose cotton and firm cotton.
flow.parent: The empty neck takes a few seconds. Loose cotton may take ten to thirty seconds. Firm cotton can take a minute or more, and the funnel may fill to the brim, so pour it in parts if you must and keep the timer running. If nothing gets through after two minutes, the plug is too tight. Loosen it a little and say so in the table.

flow.do: Divide each packed time by the empty time. Ask your child what the fine gaps did to the flow. They write what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: How many times as long did the loose cotton take? And the firm cotton? What do fine gaps do to a flow?
flow.kid: How many times as long did each one take? What do fine gaps do to a flow?
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the Slow Sieve test show.

ask.q: After the water came through the firm cotton, did it rush or drip?
good: It only dripped.
It had lost its push.

ask.q: Suppose that water then had to travel on to every part of a body. What would help?
good: Another pump after the cotton.
A push before the cotton and another after it.

check.q: Water that has passed through firmly packed cotton comes out in slow drips. What has the cotton taken away?
options: Most of the push behind the water
check.why: All the water still comes through, but rubbing past so many fine threads uses up the push behind it. Blood loses its push in the fine tubes of a gill in the same way. If you picked 'most of the water', check the bowl. The water is all there.

flow.do: Put three chairs in a triangle. Two are gill hearts and one is the main heart. Your child is the blood. They walk from the 'body' to a gill heart and squeeze past you, the gill. Then they go to the main heart and back to the body. At each heart they clap once for the push. Then explain.
flow.say: You are the blood, coming back from the body, tired and slow. Go to a gill heart. Clap. Squeeze through the gill. Go to the main heart. Clap. Now off to the body.
flow.kid: You are the blood. Clap at a gill heart. Squeeze through the gill. Clap at the main heart.
flow.context: In this step you walk the path of blood through an octopus's three hearts.
flow.parent: After the walk, explain. Each gill heart pushes blood through the fine tubes of one gill. The blood comes out slow, as the water came out of the cotton. The main heart then gives it a fresh push to the whole body. A fish has one heart for both jobs, so a fish's blood reaches the body with little push left. Your heart has two halves that do these two jobs, the right half for the lungs and the left half for the body. An octopus and a human solved the same problem in two separate ways.
flow.think: Your heart is one organ with two pumps in it. An octopus has three separate hearts. What might be good or bad about each?

activities.title: Fifteen Animals, Five Groups
activities.context: In this activity you sort fifteen animals without backbones in your own way first. Then you sort them again using five body clues that scientists use, and see which animals end up together. You will find out which animals are closer relatives than they look.
activities.record: Keep the fifteen slips in their five groups, or copy the groups into a notebook. Write down the one result that surprised you most.

setup.art: Fifteen paper slips on a table, each with an animal's name, such as 'octopus', 'ant', 'coral' and 'starfish'.
setup.caption: 1. Write fifteen animal names on fifteen slips.

setup.art: A child pushing the slips into three heaps of her own choosing.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them in your own way. Say what your rule is.

setup.art: The slips now in five rows under five small headings, with 'octopus' next to 'garden snail'.
setup.caption: 3. Sort them again with the five body clues. Who ended up together?

flow.do: Write these names on fifteen slips: bath sponge, jellyfish, coral, sea anemone, garden snail, mussel, squid, octopus, ant, prawn, spider, crab, starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber. Ask your child to sort them into groups in any way they like, and to say the rule.
flow.say: None of these fifteen animals has a backbone. Sort them into groups in any way that makes sense to you. Then tell me your rule.
flow.kid: Sort the fifteen animals into groups, your own way.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fifteen Animals, Five Groups. You sort the animals in your own way.

good: Where they live.
Whether they have legs.
Hard ones and soft ones.
Any clear rule is a good answer.

flow.parent: There is no wrong sort here. Children often sort by home, such as sea and land, or by legs. Note the rule, because you will compare it with the scientists' rule.

flow.do: Read the five clues one at a time. After each clue, your child pulls out the animals that fit. Clue 1: a body full of pores, with no mouth. Clue 2: a soft body with one opening and stinging tentacles. Clue 3: a soft body with a mantle (a flap of skin that wraps the body), and usually a foot and a shell. Clue 4: a hard outer skeleton and jointed legs. Clue 5: five matching parts and tube feet.
flow.say: Now sort them by how the body is built. Listen to each clue and pull out the animals that fit.
flow.kid: Listen to each body clue. Pull out the animals that fit that clue.
flow.context: In this step of Fifteen Animals, Five Groups you sort the animals again by five body clues.
flow.parent: The answers are: sponges, 1 (bath sponge). Cnidarians, 3 (jellyfish, coral, sea anemone). Molluscs, 4 (garden snail, mussel, squid, octopus). Arthropods, 4 (ant, prawn, spider, crab). Echinoderms, 3 (starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber). If your child does not know an animal, look at a picture together before deciding.

flow.do: Look at the five groups together. Ask what your child notices and what they wonder. Point to the octopus beside the garden snail and ask what the two could share.
flow.say: What do you notice about who ended up together? What do you wonder? The octopus is with the snail. What could those two share?
flow.kid: Look at the five groups. What could an octopus and a snail share?
flow.context: This is the last step of Fifteen Animals, Five Groups. You look at who ended up together and ask why.

ask.q: What do you notice, and what do you wonder?
good: The octopus and the snail are in one group.
The ant and the crab are together though one lives on land.
Why is a sea cucumber with a starfish?
Which group has the most animals in the world?

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. The explanations and the Boss or Hand test come next. Keep the question about the octopus and the snail open.
flow.think: An octopus is in the snail's group. A snail has a tiny brain. So how did the octopus come to be so clever?

activities.title: Fifty Beans: where are an octopus's nerve cells?
activities.context: In this activity fifty beans stand for all the nerve cells of an octopus, and you place them on a picture of her body. You will see where she keeps most of her nerve cells, the tiny cells that carry messages around the body. Then you do the same for a human and compare the two pictures.
activities.safety: Dry beans can choke a child under five, so keep them out of reach of very young children.
activities.record: Keep the two drawings. On each, write how many beans went in the head and how many went elsewhere.

setup.art: A large simple drawing of an octopus on a sheet of paper, with a round head and eight arms spread out like a star, and a heap of fifty chana beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a big octopus with eight arms. Count out 50 beans.

setup.art: The octopus drawing with eighteen beans on the head and four beans along each arm.
setup.caption: 2. Put 18 beans in the head and 4 on each arm.

setup.art: A simple outline of a person with almost all fifty beans heaped on the head.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a person. Put almost all 50 beans in the head. Compare.

flow.do: Your child draws a large octopus with eight arms. Or they make one from a bowl and eight paper strips. Then they count out 50 beans. Say that the beans stand for all her nerve cells, about 500 million. Ask where they think most of the beans should go, and why.
flow.say: These 50 beans are all the nerve cells of one octopus. Each bean stands for 10 million. Where do you think most of them are? Why?
flow.kid: The 50 beans are an octopus's nerve cells. Where do you think most belong? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fifty Beans. You guess where an octopus's nerve cells are.
flow.parent: Most children put nearly all the beans in the head, because that is where our own are.

flow.do: Now place the beans as scientists have counted them. Put 18 beans in the head and 4 beans along each of the eight arms. Count the beans in the arms together.
flow.say: About two thirds are in the arms. Put 18 in the head and 4 on each arm. How many are in the arms altogether?
flow.kid: Put 18 beans in the head. Put 4 on each arm. Count the arm beans.
flow.context: In this step of Fifty Beans you place the beans where an octopus's nerve cells really are.

check.q: Each arm has 4 beans, and there are 8 arms. How many of the 50 beans are in the arms?
check.why: 8 times 4 is 32. That is 32 out of 50, a little under two thirds. So well over half of an octopus's nerve cells are outside her head. If you got 12, you added 8 and 4 where you needed to multiply.

flow.parent: The real share is a rough figure, about two thirds. Of the beans in the head, most stand for the two large parts behind the eyes that deal with seeing.

flow.do: Your child draws a simple person on the second sheet. A circle for the head and a line for the body is enough. Say that a human has about 86 billion nerve cells, and almost all are in the brain. They move the 50 beans to show that. Compare the two drawings.
flow.say: A human has far more nerve cells, and almost all are in the brain. Show that with the same 50 beans. How are the two pictures different?
flow.kid: Now make a person: a circle for the head and a line for the body. Put almost all the beans in the head. How do the pictures differ?
flow.context: This is the last step of Fifty Beans. You compare where a human's nerve cells are with where an octopus's are.

ask.q: What might an animal gain by keeping most nerve cells in the arms?
good: The arm can act fast without waiting for the brain.
The brain has fewer orders to give.
Each arm can do its own job.

flow.parent: For a true scale, a human would need 8,600 beans for every 50 of the octopus. The point here is where the cells are, not how many.
flow.think: If you had to draw where 'you' are in your body, where would you draw it? Where would an octopus draw it?

activities.title: Feel or Taste? What a fingertip can and cannot tell
activities.context: In this activity you try to tell sugar water from salt water with a fingertip, and then with your tongue. An octopus's sucker senses touch and chemicals together, and this shows what that would add to a finger. You will find out whether a fingertip alone can tell sweet from salty.

materials.item: steel tumblers, each half full of drinking water at room temperature
paper and a pencil for the score

activities.record: Write how many of six finger guesses were right, and how many of two tongue guesses were right.

setup.art: Two identical steel tumblers of water on a table, a spoon of sugar going into one and a spoon of salt into the other.
setup.caption: 1. Stir sugar into one tumbler and salt into the other.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut dipping one fingertip into a tumbler held by a parent.
setup.caption: 2. Eyes shut. Dip a fingertip. Sweet or salty? Guess six times.

setup.art: The same child touching a wet fingertip to her tongue and smiling.
setup.caption: 3. Now touch the wet finger to your tongue. Guess twice.

flow.do: Stir a teaspoon of sugar into one tumbler and a teaspoon of salt into the other. Stir until nothing is left at the bottom. Ask your child whether a fingertip will be able to tell them apart, and why.
flow.say: One has sugar and one has salt. With your eyes shut, could your finger tell which is which? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One has sugar. One has salt. Can your finger tell them apart? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel or Taste. You guess whether a fingertip can tell sugar water from salt water.
flow.parent: Stir until both are clear, so that grains do not give the answer away.

flow.do: Your child shuts their eyes. Hold out one tumbler at a time, six times, in an order you choose in secret. Each time they dip a clean fingertip and say 'sugar' or 'salt'. Keep the score. They dry the finger between dips.
flow.say: Eyes shut. Dip your finger. Sugar or salt? I will not tell you if you are right until the end.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Dip a fingertip. Say sugar or salt. Do it six times.
flow.context: In this step of Feel or Taste you test what a fingertip can tell.
flow.parent: By guessing alone, a person gets about 3 right out of 6. A score of 2, 3 or 4 means the finger could not tell. Use each tumbler three times so the test is even.

flow.do: Now your child dips a finger and touches it to the tongue, twice, and says which is which. Compare the two scores. Ask what the finger could tell and what it could not.
flow.say: Now touch your wet finger to your tongue. Which one is this?
flow.kid: Touch the wet finger to your tongue. Which is which?
flow.context: This is the last step of Feel or Taste. You compare what a finger and a tongue can tell.

ask.q: What did your fingertip know about the water, and what did it not know?
good: It knew the water was wet and cool.
It did not know what was dissolved in it.
The tongue knew at once.

flow.parent: After your child answers, explain. Your fingertip has cells that sense touch, pressure and warmth, but none that sense sugar or salt. Your tongue has both kinds. In 2020, Lena van Giesen's team found both kinds in the skin of an octopus's suckers. So an arm in a dark crack can sense that it has touched a crab.
flow.think: If your fingers could taste, what would you know about a mango before you ever lifted it to your mouth?

activities.title: The Inside-Out Thread: a model of a stinging cell
activities.context: In this activity a balloon tucked inside a plastic bottle shoots out when you squeeze the bottle. It is a model of the thread inside a stinging cell of a jellyfish or a coral, which turns inside out as it fires. You will see how a thread can shoot out by turning inside out.

materials.item: a soft empty plastic bottle, about half a litre or one litre

activities.safety: A burst or loose balloon can choke a young child. A grown-up fits the balloon, and children under eight do not put balloons in their mouths.
activities.record: Draw the model before and after the squeeze, or take two photos. Name the capsule, the thread and what set it off.

setup.art: An empty soft plastic bottle with the mouth of a balloon stretched over the bottle's mouth and the rest of the balloon hanging outside.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch the mouth of a balloon over the mouth of a bottle.

setup.art: A finger pushing the balloon down inside the neck of the bottle so that it hangs inside.
setup.caption: 2. Push the balloon inside the bottle with a finger.

setup.art: Two hands squeezing the bottle hard and the balloon popping out of the top, turned inside out.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze the bottle hard and fast. Watch the balloon.

flow.do: Stretch the mouth of the balloon over the mouth of the bottle. Push the rest of the balloon down inside the bottle with a finger. Ask your child what will happen when the bottle is squeezed hard, and why.
flow.say: The balloon is tucked inside. What will happen when you squeeze the bottle hard and fast? Why?
flow.kid: The balloon is inside the bottle. What happens if you squeeze hard? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Inside-Out Thread. You set up the model and guess.
flow.parent: The balloon's mouth must grip the bottle's mouth all round. If it slips off, hold it in place with a rubber band. An easy way to get the balloon inside is to squeeze the bottle a little, fit the balloon, and let go.

flow.do: Your child squeezes the bottle hard and fast with both hands. The balloon turns inside out and pops out of the top. Push it back in and do it again, three times.
flow.say: Squeeze hard and fast. What did the balloon do? Push it back in and try again.
flow.kid: Squeeze the bottle hard and fast. What did the balloon do? Try it three times.
flow.context: In this step of the Inside-Out Thread you fire the model and watch what the balloon does.

ask.q: Which side of the balloon is on the outside after it pops out?
good: The side that was inside before.
It turned inside out.

flow.do: Explain what each part stands for. The bottle is the capsule. The balloon is the hollow thread. Your squeeze is the pressure stored inside the capsule. Ask how the model differs from the real thing.
flow.say: The bottle is the capsule in a stinging cell. The balloon is the thread. The real thread fires in under a millionth of a second. How is our model different?
flow.kid: The bottle is the capsule. The balloon is the thread. How is the real one different?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Inside-Out Thread. You match the model to a real stinging cell.

check.q: A stinging cell's thread is packed inside a capsule. How does the thread come out?
options: It turns inside out as it shoots out
It uncoils like a rope being thrown
check.why: The hollow thread is tucked inside itself, like your balloon in the bottle. Pressure pushes it out inside first. That is why barbs hidden inside the packed thread end up on the outside. If you picked the rope, that is the usual guess, but the thread is a tube, and it turns inside out.

flow.parent: In the real capsule the pressure is already stored, and a touch on a tiny trigger hair opens the lid. The real thread is far thinner than a hair and is used only once. Our model is slower, bigger, squeezed from outside, and can be used again.

activities.title: Many Feet, No Boss: carry a plate together without a word
activities.context: In this activity two people carry a plate with a lemon on it around a chair, once with one person giving every order and once in silence. A starfish has hundreds of tube feet and no brain, and this shows one way that many feet can work together. You will find out whether a team can move well with no one giving orders.

materials.item: a lemon or a small ball

activities.record: Write the time for each round and how many times the lemon fell.

setup.art: A parent and child facing each other, each holding one side of a steel plate with a lemon in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a plate between you, with a lemon on it.

setup.art: The pair walking round a chair while the child calls out orders.
setup.caption: 2. Round 1: one of you orders every step. Walk round the chair and back.

setup.art: The same pair walking round the chair in silence, both looking at the lemon.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2: nobody speaks. Both of you feel the plate. Compare the times.

flow.do: Stand facing each other and hold the plate between you with the lemon in the middle. Mark a start line and put a chair three big steps away. Ask which round will be quicker and steadier, and why.
flow.say: We will carry this round the chair twice. Once you order every step. Once nobody speaks. Which will go better? Why?
flow.kid: Which round will go better: with orders, or in silence? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Many Feet, No Boss. You set up and guess.

flow.do: Round 1. Your child gives every order, such as 'left foot', 'stop' and 'turn', and you move only when told. Time the trip and count how often the lemon falls. Round 2. Nobody speaks. Both of you watch the lemon and feel the plate. Time and count again.
flow.say: Round 1. Tell me every step. I move only when you say. Round 2. No words. Feel the plate and watch the lemon.
flow.kid: Round 1: order every step. Round 2: say nothing and feel the plate.
flow.context: In this step of Many Feet, No Boss you carry the plate with orders and then in silence.
flow.parent: Walk slowly. In round 1, wait for each order even when you can see what is needed.

flow.do: Compare the two rounds. Ask how each of you knew what the other was doing in the silent round. Then explain how a starfish's tube feet work together.
flow.say: In the silent round, how did you know which way I was going? What carried the message between us?
flow.kid: With no words, how did you know where I was going?
flow.context: This is the last step of Many Feet, No Boss. You work out what carried the message in the silent round.

ask.q: What carried the message between you when nobody spoke?
good: The plate. I felt it tilt and pull.
I watched the lemon.
I felt which way you were moving.

flow.parent: After your child answers, explain. The plate carried the message. Each of you felt its pull and tilt and adjusted. A starfish's tube feet are all joined to one body. When some feet pull the body one way, the others feel that pull and step the same way. A ring of nerves and a nerve in each arm help to settle which arm leads. Scientists are still working out how much is done by the nerves and how much by the pull of the body.
flow.think: Where else do many workers move together with nobody giving orders?

projects.title: Five Groups Field Book: who can you find in four days?
projects.context: In this project you make a small book with one page for each of the five big groups of animals without backbones. Over four days you hunt for a living member, a trace or a picture of each group, at home, in the market and in books. You will find out which groups are easy to meet at home and which are not.

materials.item: a notebook, or five sheets of paper stapled together
a magnifying glass, if you have one

projects.safety: Look at spiders, centipedes and anything found on a beach without touching. Wash your hands after handling shells or shellfish from a market.

schedule.what: Head five pages with the five groups and their body clues. Hunt at home for arthropods.
Hunt for molluscs: a snail after rain, or shells in the house, in a board game or at a fish stall.
Find pictures of a sponge, a cnidarian and an echinoderm in a book or with a grown-up online. Draw one of each.
Count what you found alive, as a trace and only as a picture. Write what the count shows.

projects.record: On each page write the group, the body clue, what you found, where, and whether it was alive, a trace such as a shell, or a picture. On the last page write the count for each group and one sentence on what it shows.

setup.art: An open notebook with a page headed 'Arthropods: hard skeleton, jointed legs' and a small drawing of an ant.
setup.caption: 1. Make one page for each of the five groups, with the body clue at the top.

setup.art: A child with a magnifying glass looking at an ant on a window sill.
setup.caption: 2. Hunt at home and in the market. Look, count, and do not harm.

setup.art: A page with a table of five rows and three columns headed 'alive', 'trace' and 'picture only', with tally marks.
setup.caption: 3. On day 4, count what you found alive, as a trace, or only as a picture.

flow.do: Your child heads five pages with the five groups and writes each body clue. Then they hunt at home for arthropods, such as ants, a mosquito, a house spider or a cockroach. They count the legs, and may draw it too.
flow.say: Make a page for each group. Today we hunt for arthropods at home. Find one, look closely, count the legs.
flow.kid: Make five pages. Find an arthropod at home. Count the legs.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Five Groups Field Book. You set up the book and look for arthropods.
flow.parent: Arthropods are nearly always there: ants on a sill, a spider in a corner, a mosquito at dusk. Dry prawns or a crab from the market count as traces.

flow.do: On day 2, hunt for molluscs. Look for a snail or a slug on a wall after rain. Look for shells in the house, such as cowries in a board game or a conch on a shelf. If your family buys from a fish stall, look for mussels, clams or squid.
flow.say: Today we look for molluscs. A snail after rain counts. So does any shell, because a mollusc built it.
flow.kid: Hunt for molluscs. A snail counts. A shell counts too, because a mollusc built it.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Five Groups Field Book. You look for molluscs and their shells.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day
flow.parent: A shell is a trace, not a living animal, so mark it as a trace. Cowrie shells are used in games such as chowka bara and pallanguzhi.

flow.do: On day 3, look for a sponge, a cnidarian (such as a jellyfish or coral) and an echinoderm (such as a starfish). In most homes these will be pictures in a book or online. Your child names one of each and writes the body clue they can see in the picture. They may draw it too.
flow.say: Today we look for the three groups who live almost only in the sea. Find a picture of each. Pick one, and point to the body clue.
flow.kid: Find a picture of a sponge, a coral or jellyfish, and a starfish. Say which body clue you can see in each.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Five Groups Field Book. You look for the three groups who live mostly in the sea.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day
flow.parent: A kitchen sponge is made in a factory and a loofah is a plant, so neither counts. A piece of coral or a dried starfish in someone's showcase is a trace. Do not buy corals, shells or dried sea animals for this, because the trade harms reefs.

flow.do: On day 4, your child counts for each group how many finds were alive, traces or pictures only. Ask why some groups were easy to find at home and others were not. They write one sentence on what the count shows.
flow.say: Count your finds. Which groups did you see alive? Which only in pictures? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Count your finds for each group: alive, a trace, or a picture.
flow.context: This is day 4 of the Five Groups Field Book. You count your finds and say what the count shows.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day

ask.q: Why did you find arthropods alive at home, but echinoderms only in pictures?
good: Echinoderms live only in the sea.
Arthropods can live on dry land because the hard skeleton keeps water in.
There are far more kinds of arthropod.

flow.parent: Most city families find living arthropods, perhaps a snail, and only pictures of the other three. That result is the finding. Sponges, cnidarians and echinoderms live in water, nearly all of them in the sea, and only arthropods and some molluscs have spread widely over land.

challenges.title: The Soft Gripper: lift things with no hard fingers
challenges.context: In this challenge you design a gripper made only of soft things that can lift a pencil, a lemon and a steel tumbler. An octopus arm has no bones, and engineers copy it to build soft robot arms.
challenges.problem: An octopus picks up shells, crabs and jars with arms that have no bones. Design and build a gripper made only of soft, bendy things. It must lift a pencil, a lemon and an empty steel tumbler off a table and hold each for five seconds. Your fingers may hold the gripper but may not touch the object.
constraints: Only soft or bendy materials may touch the object: cloth, string, rubber bands, balloons, paper, tape or a sock.
No spoons, tongs, sticks or bare fingers on the object.
The same gripper, or two at most, must lift all three objects.
You have 30 minutes, and each object must stay up for a count of five.

materials.item: a pencil, a lemon and an empty steel tumbler
soft things: a sock, strips of cloth, string, rubber bands, sticky tape, paper
paper and a pencil for drawing the design

challenges.safety: A burst balloon can choke a young child. Keep balloons and rubber bands away from children under five.
general: Wrap a strip of cloth once round the object and twist the two ends together until it grips.
Make a loop of string, drop it over the object and pull it tight.
Lay the object on a cloth and lift the corners, like a bundle.
creative: Push a balloon into the tumbler and blow it up inside. The balloon presses on the wall, and lifting the balloon lifts the tumbler.
Roll sticky tape into a ring with the sticky side out and wind it round a sock on your hand.
Make three cloth 'arms' on one ring of string, so that pulling the ring closes all three round a lemon.
Stretch a wide rubber band round the tumbler, and hook a loop of string under the band as a handle.
challenges.your_turn: Design a soft gripper for a job a hard hand does badly, such as picking up a ripe tomato, a raw egg or a soft toy. Draw it or build a small model, and say which part of an octopus arm gave you the idea.

setup.art: A pencil, a lemon and a steel tumbler in a row on a table, with a sock, cloth strips, string, rubber bands and two balloons beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Set out the three objects and your soft materials.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a cloth strip wrapped round a lemon with the ends twisted.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a design before you build.

setup.art: A child lifting a steel tumbler by a balloon blown up inside it.
setup.caption: 3. Build, test on all three objects, and change what fails.

flow.do: Read the problem and the rules aloud. Ask your child how an octopus arm holds things with no bones. Ask what their own gripper could copy from it.
flow.say: An octopus arm has no bones. How does it hold a shell? What could your gripper copy from that?
flow.kid: How does an arm with no bones hold a shell? What could you copy?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Soft Gripper challenge. You think about how a boneless arm holds things.

ask.q: What are the ways a soft arm can hold something?
good: Wrapping right round it.
Sticking on with suckers.
Stiffening after it has wrapped.

flow.do: Your child plans one or two designs. They can draw them or lay the soft things out. They say how each will hold the pencil, the lemon and the tumbler. Do not suggest a design yet.
flow.say: Plan your gripper. Draw it or lay out the parts. Show me how it holds a thin thing, a round thing and a hollow thing.
flow.kid: Plan your gripper. How will it hold each of the three things?
flow.context: In this step of the Soft Gripper challenge you draw your design.
flow.parent: The three objects are chosen to be awkward in different ways. A thin pencil slips out of a loose wrap, a lemon rolls, and a tumbler is wide and smooth.

flow.do: Your child builds the gripper and tests it on each object. Each lift must last a count of five. After each failure, ask what slipped and why, and let them change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Build it and try the pencil first. Count to five. What slipped? Change one thing and test again.
flow.kid: Build it. Test each object for a count of five. Change one thing if it fails.
flow.context: In this step of the Soft Gripper challenge you build, test and improve your gripper.
flow.parent: Stay close while balloons are being blown up. If your child is stuck after ten minutes, read out one idea from the usual solutions.

flow.do: Ask your child which object was hardest and what change helped most. Read the creative solutions together and compare them with your child's own. Then tell them about Cecilia Laschi's robot arm.
flow.say: Which object was hardest? What change helped most? Here are some other ideas. Which is closest to yours?
flow.kid: Which object was hardest? What change helped most? Compare with the other ideas.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Soft Gripper challenge. You look back at what worked.
flow.parent: From 2009, Cecilia Laschi and her team in Pisa in Italy built a soft robot arm of silicone, copied from an octopus arm. Cables and springs inside it did the work of muscles. Because the arm was soft, its own body did part of the work that a computer would otherwise have to plan.
flow.think: A hard robot hand must be told exactly where its fingers are. Why might a soft arm need fewer orders?

items.p: Which body clue marks a sponge?
opts: Pores all over and no mouth
items.why: A sponge's body is a wall of cells full of pores, with no mouth or gut. Stinging tentacles mark a cnidarian, and jointed legs mark an arthropod.

items.p: Match each group to its body clue.
items.why: Each group is known by how the body is built, and not by where the animal lives or how big the animal is.

items.p: Sort each animal: mollusc or arthropod?
items.why: Snails, mussels and cuttlefish have a soft body under a mantle. Prawns, spiders and barnacles have jointed legs and an outer skeleton. The barnacle's legs are hidden inside the shell.

items.p: A sponge has no nerve cells, yet the whole body can squeeze together.
items.why: True. Sponge cells pass chemical signals to their neighbours, and the squeeze spreads slowly through the body. It can take half an hour.

items.p: Filtered water leaves a sponge through a large opening called the ____.
items.why: Water comes in through thousands of small pores and goes out through the osculum.

items.p: Why does a sponge push used water out in one strong jet?
opts: So the used water travels far away
items.why: A strong jet carries the used water away, so the sponge does not pull the same water in again. A sponge stays fixed in one place and does not swim.

items.p: What sets off a stinging cell?
opts: A touch on the cell's trigger
items.why: Each stinging cell fires by itself when the trigger is touched. No order comes from a brain or from anywhere else, and even a tentacle washed up on a beach can still sting.

items.p: A coral is a rock that small animals live on.
items.why: False. The coral is the animals. Each polyp builds a cup of limestone under their body, and the cups of many polyps make the rock.

items.p: Put in order the path of blood in an octopus, starting when it comes back from the body.
a: Blood comes back from the body
It is pushed through a gill and picks up oxygen
It is pushed out to the body
items.why: A gill heart pushes the blood through the fine tubes of a gill. The main heart then gives it a fresh push to the body.

items.p: The oxygen carrier in octopus blood holds the metal ____.
items.why: Haemocyanin holds copper and is blue when it carries oxygen. Our haemoglobin holds iron and is red.

items.p: In Way 1, three tries took 26, 31 and 17 seconds. What is the total?
items.why: 26 and 31 make 57, and 17 more make 74 seconds. Adding the three tries gives one number for each way, so the ways are easy to compare.

items.p: In the Boss or Hand test, why is the coin moved before every try?
opts: So remembering the last place does not help
So the boss cannot see the coin
items.why: If the coin stayed put, the hand could go straight back to it from memory. Then you would be testing memory, and not the three ways of sharing the work.

items.p: An octopus arm in a dark crack finds a crab that her eyes cannot see. Explain how.
items.a: The suckers sense touch and also the chemicals of the crab. The arm's own nerve cord works out the grip and the bends. The brain only needs to send the arm to the crack.
items.why: A strong answer names the suckers' sensing and the arm's own nerve cord, and gives the brain a smaller job.

items.p: Draw a sponge shaped like a vase. Add arrows to show where water goes in and where it comes out.
items.a: Many small arrows going in through the side wall, and one large arrow coming out of the wide opening at the top.
items.why: A strong drawing shows many small ways in and one large way out, and labels the osculum.

items.p: Does each octopus arm have a mind of its own?

views.says: Yes. Two thirds of her nerve cells are in the arms, and an arm cut off from the brain still reaches.
No. Her brain chooses which arm to send and where, and learns from what an arm feels.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What would you want to find out next?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and names something to test, such as whether an arm can learn something that the other arms then know.
items.why: Both views accept the same experiments. They differ on what should count as a mind.

items.p: A cuttlefish is grouped with snails. Why?
opts: Both have a mantle, a radula and a soft body
items.why: Groups follow the body plan. A cuttlefish has a mantle, a radula and a soft body with no segments, as a snail has. Many land snails do not live in water, and a cuttlefish is fast.

items.p: Which of these animals is your closest relative?
items.why: Echinoderms are on the same big branch of the family tree as animals with backbones. Crabs and octopuses are on another branch. Looks do not show this, but the growing egg and the DNA do.

items.p: Every echinoderm lives in the sea.
items.why: True. Their tube feet are filled with sea water, and no echinoderm lives in fresh water or on land.

items.p: Why do arthropods have so many kinds of tools on one body?
opts: Limbs on each segment can change shape and job
items.why: An arthropod's body is a row of segments, each with a pair of limbs. Over time, limbs on different segments became jaws, feelers, claws, legs and paddles.

items.p: A starfish's tube foot stretches out when ____ is pushed into it.
items.why: Muscles squeeze a small bulb, and the water in it is pushed into the tube foot. Water cannot be squashed smaller, so the foot must lengthen.

items.p: Sort each animal by how the nerve cells are arranged.
items.why: Each group arranges nerve cells in a different way. The octopus also has a nerve cord in each arm that holds most of her nerve cells.

items.p: Put in order how a sponge feeds.
a: Water is pulled in through small pores
The collars catch bacteria from the water
Crawling cells carry the food round the body
Used water leaves through the osculum
items.why: The beating threads make the flow, the collars do the catching, and other cells do the carrying. No mouth or gut is needed.

items.p: Match each octopus part to its job.
pairs: squirts water for a fast escape
items.why: These are mollusc parts put to new uses. A snail's mantle makes a shell, and an octopus's mantle is a muscular bag that pumps water.

items.p: Fifty beans stand for an octopus's nerve cells. 4 go on each of 8 arms. How many are left for the head?
items.why: 8 times 4 is 32 beans in the arms. 50 take away 32 leaves 18 for the head. So fewer than half are in the head.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Snail, mussel, squid, crab.
items.a: Crab. A crab is an arthropod with jointed legs. The other three are molluscs.
items.why: Snail, mussel and squid share the mollusc plan of a soft body under a mantle. A crab's hard shell is an outer skeleton that is shed, which is a different thing from a mollusc's shell.

items.p: Why does an octopus need a strong push from her main heart?
items.a: Her blood has just come through the fine tubes of the gills and lost its push. Her blue blood also carries less oxygen than ours, so it must keep moving well to supply her body.
items.why: A strong answer gives both reasons: the gills take away the push, and haemocyanin carries less oxygen in each drop.

items.p: In Sea Soup, milk passed every filter. What does that tell you about how a sponge catches bacteria?
items.a: Bacteria are about as small as the droplets in milk, so a sponge's filter must have gaps far finer than cloth. The collar cells' tiny fingers make such gaps.
items.why: A strong answer says a filter stops only what is bigger than its gaps, and that the sponge's gaps must be very fine.

items.p: Draw the path of blood through an octopus's three hearts. Use arrows.
items.a: A loop: body, two gill hearts side by side, a gill after each, then one main heart, then back to the body.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the gill hearts before the gills and the main heart after them.

items.p: An octopus arm cut off from the brain can still make the normal reaching movement.
items.why: True. When the arm's nerve cord was given a small signal, the arm reached out in the usual wave. The pattern is held in the arm.

items.p: Is a coral colony one animal or many?

views.says: One. The polyps are joined by living tissue, share their food, and all grew from one first polyp.
Many. Each polyp has a mouth and tentacles, and a broken-off piece can live and grow.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Can both be right?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer gives a reason, and may say that 'one' and 'many' are both true, depending on what you count.
items.why: The facts are not in doubt. The question is what we mean by 'one animal', and scientists use both ways of counting.

items.p: Why does a fish's blood reach the body with little push left?
opts: One heart pushes it through gills and body in a row
A fish's heart is very weak
A fish has no blood tubes
items.why: A fish has one pump. The blood loses most of its push in the fine tubes of the gills, and then has to travel on round the body with what is left.

items.p: Which part of your body does the job of an octopus's gill hearts?
opts: The right half of the heart
The left half of the heart
items.why: The right half of your heart pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left half pumps it to the body, as the octopus's main heart does.

items.p: On a small plate, the hand alone beat 'aim only'. What is the best explanation?
opts: A small plate is quick to search without help
The boss gave a wrong aim on purpose
The hand could see the coin
items.why: The aim saves searching time. On a small plate there is little searching to save, so the time spent listening can cost more than it saves. On a very large plate the aim would matter much more.

items.p: Scientists use only the look of adult animals to work out the animal family tree.
items.why: False. Adult looks can mislead. A starfish looks nothing like us. Scientists also compare how eggs grow, and above all the DNA.

items.p: An octopus's suckers grip her own skin as readily as they grip a crab.
items.why: False. A chemical in octopus skin stops the suckers from gripping. This helps to keep eight arms from holding on to each other.

items.p: Put in order how a stinging cell fires.
a: A hollow thread lies coiled in a capsule under pressure
The lid of the capsule opens
The thread turns inside out and shoots into the prey
items.why: The pressure is stored before the touch, which is why the firing can be so fast. The whole firing takes less than a millionth of a second.

items.p: The closest single-celled relatives of animals look like a sponge's ____ cells.
items.why: Choanoflagellates have a thread inside a collar of tiny fingers, as a sponge's collar cells have. Their DNA shows they are the closest living relatives of animals.

items.p: A sponge pumps 2 litres of water every minute. How many litres is that in one hour?
items.why: There are 60 minutes in an hour, and 60 times 2 is 120 litres. A sponge the size of a water bottle can pump more than a large drum of water in an hour.

items.p: Sort each fact: true of sponges, of cnidarians, or of both?
items.why: Both groups are animals of the sea with simple-looking bodies, but a cnidarian has tissues, a mouth, muscles and nerve cells, and a sponge has none of these.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Gill heart, mantle, funnel, tube foot.
items.a: Tube foot. A tube foot belongs to an echinoderm. The other three are parts of an octopus.
items.why: A tube foot is worked by water pressure and is found only in starfish and their relatives.

items.p: 'An animal needs a brain to learn.' Give one piece of evidence against this claim.
items.a: Box jellyfish have no brain, yet in a 2023 study they learned to steer round obstacles after a few bumps. A sponge has no nerve cells and still squeezes when the water is dirty.
items.why: A strong answer names an animal with no brain and says what that animal did that shows learning or a fitting response.

items.p: Design a test: does an octopus use sight to guide one arm to food? Say what you keep the same.
items.a: Give her a clear maze with food in one of three boxes that she can see but not smell. Then cover the maze so she cannot see in. Keep the maze, the food and the octopus the same.
items.why: A strong answer changes only whether she can see, and takes away smell and taste as clues. Tamar Gutnick's team did this in 2011.

items.p: Why is 'invertebrates' not one family of animals?
items.a: The word only says that an animal lacks a backbone. It covers many separate branches. Starfish are closer relatives of animals with backbones than of crabs or snails.
items.why: A strong answer says the group is defined by what is missing, and gives the starfish as an example of a branch nearer to us.

items.p: Draw an octopus arm cut open along its length. Show the nerve cord and what sits beside each sucker.
items.a: A long arm with a cord down the middle and a small knot of nerve cells, a ganglion, beside every sucker, each joined to the cord.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one knot for each sucker and labels the nerve cord and a ganglion.

items.p: Does an octopus have one stream of experience, or several?

views.says: One. Her brain gathers what matters from all eight arms and decides for the whole body.
Perhaps several. Each arm senses and acts, and little of that news seems to reach the brain.

items.ask: Which do you find more likely? What would you want to test?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer gives a reason and admits that nobody can yet measure experience from outside.
items.why: This is a real open question. The experiments show what the arms and the brain do, but not what it is like for the octopus.

quiz.p: Which group has a hard outer skeleton and legs that bend at joints?
quiz.why: Jointed legs and an outer skeleton mark the arthropods. If you chose molluscs, remember that a snail's shell is a house the body sits in, and a mollusc has no jointed legs.

quiz.p: Which of these animals is a mollusc?
quiz.why: A squid has a mantle and a soft body with no segments. A starfish is an echinoderm. A barnacle looks like a shellfish but has jointed legs inside, so the barnacle is an arthropod.

quiz.p: How does a sponge get food?
opts: By pulling water through pores and filtering
quiz.why: Collar cells beat their threads, pull water through the body and catch bacteria. Tentacles belong to cnidarians. Making food from sunlight is what plants and algae do, and it is why people once took sponges for plants.

quiz.p: Why does a sponge count as an animal?
opts: Many cells, eats living things, makes eggs and sperm
quiz.why: A sponge is built of many cells, feeds on bacteria and other living specks, and makes eggs and sperm. An adult sponge stays in one place and has no nerve cells at all, so moving and brains are not what makes an animal.

quiz.p: What happens when reef corals turn white in a sea that stays too hot?
opts: The tiny algae inside them are lost
quiz.why: The algae living in the coral's cells give much of the colour and most of the food. In long heat the partnership breaks down and the algae go. Limestone does not melt in warm water.

quiz.p: Which parts does an octopus share with a garden snail?
opts: Jointed legs and a hard skeleton
quiz.why: Both are molluscs, with a mantle over the body and a toothed ribbon in the mouth. The octopus's ancestors lost the shell. Jointed legs belong to arthropods.

quiz.p: What pushes a starfish's tube foot out?
quiz.why: Muscles squeeze a bulb of water, and the water stretches the foot. Echinoderms have no bones in the tube feet, and they live under water, where there is no air to blow.

quiz.p: What do an octopus's two gill hearts do?
quiz.why: Each gill heart pushes blood through the fine tubes of one gill. The main heart then sends the blood round the whole body, arms included.

quiz.p: The same amount of octopus blood carries more oxygen than human blood.
quiz.why: False. Octopus blood carries several times less. That is one reason she needs a strong main heart to keep it moving.

quiz.p: Where are most of an octopus's nerve cells?
opts: In the brain in her head
quiz.why: About two thirds are in the nerve cords of the arms. If you chose the brain, that is true of a human, and it is the habit this unit asks you to question.

quiz.p: In the Boss or Hand test, why is ordering every move slow?
opts: Each order takes time, and the boss is not touching
The hand gets tired of listening
quiz.why: Words are slow, many orders are needed for one small act, and the boss does not know what the fingers are touching. Giving only the aim lets the hand use what it feels.

quiz.p: Which animal has a nerve net and no brain?
quiz.why: Cnidarians such as sea anemones and jellyfish have nerve cells spread as a net. An ant and an octopus both have brains.

open_questions.q: How do an octopus's brain and arms share their decisions?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments show that arms can act alone and that the brain can direct one arm. Nobody has yet recorded both at work in a freely moving octopus and traced who decides what.

open_questions.q: Does an octopus have one stream of experience, or several?
open_questions.why_open: Experience cannot be measured from outside, and an octopus's nerve cells are arranged so differently from ours that our own case is a poor guide.

open_questions.q: How does a sponge pass a signal through the whole body with no nerve cells?
open_questions.why_open: Chemical signals between cells are known to be involved, but the whole path from first cell to last has not been traced.

open_questions.q: Which branched off the animal family tree first, sponges or comb jellies?
open_questions.why_open: A 2023 study of chromosomes points to comb jellies, but some DNA studies still point to sponges, and scientists have not all agreed.

open_questions.q: Why do echinoderms have five parts?
open_questions.why_open: Fossils show early echinoderms with other numbers. Nobody knows why five won, or whether five has any special advantage.

open_questions.q: How did single cells first come to live together as one animal body?
open_questions.why_open: It happened more than 600 million years ago and left almost no fossils. Living relatives such as choanoflagellates give clues, but scientists read those clues differently.

maths.problem: In Way 1 of the Boss or Hand test, the boss gave 14 orders, and each order took about 2 seconds to say and obey. In Way 3 the boss gave 1 order of about 3 seconds, and the hand then needed 6 seconds. How much time did Way 3 save?
maths.answer: 19 seconds. Way 1 took about 28 seconds and Way 3 took about 9 seconds.
maths.explain: 14 orders at 2 seconds each is 28 seconds. In Way 3, 3 seconds and 6 seconds make 9 seconds. 28 take away 9 is 19. Nearly all of the time in Way 1 went on saying and obeying orders.
maths.context: In the Boss or Hand test, a hand with shut eyes finds a coin on a plate, either with every move ordered or with only the aim given.
maths.why_maths: Counting the orders and timing them shows where the time went, which the total time alone does not show.

maths.problem: An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, and about two thirds of them are in her eight arms. About how many nerve cells are in one arm?
maths.explain: Two thirds of 500 million is about 333 million. Shared between 8 arms, that is 333 divided by 8, which is a little under 42 million. A honeybee's whole brain has about 1 million nerve cells, so one octopus arm has about as many as 40 bees.
maths.context: In Fifty Beans, you placed beans on a drawing of an octopus to show where her nerve cells are.
maths.why_maths: Working out the share for one arm, and comparing it with a whole bee, shows that an arm has enough nerve cells to do real work alone.

maths.problem: The chart shows one child's three tries for each way in the Boss or Hand test. One try in Way 2 took far longer than the other two. What could explain it, and should that try be thrown away?
maths.answer: The coin may have been hidden in the last place the hand searched. The try should stay. It shows that searching alone depends on luck.
maths.explain: The Way 2 tries were 9, 11 and 38 seconds. A hand searching without an aim finds the coin quickly if it starts near it and slowly if it starts far away. That spread is a real feature of searching alone. The Way 3 tries were 6, 7 and 5 seconds, which are close together, because the aim takes the luck out.
maths.context: In the Boss or Hand test, each way of finding the coin is tried three times, with the coin in a new place each time.
maths.why_maths: Looking at how spread out the times are, and not only at the total, tells you which way is dependable.

maths.problem: Suppose a sponge the size of a 1 litre bottle pumps 2 litres of sea water every minute. How many litres does the sponge pump in a day? A rooftop water tank holds 1,000 litres. About how many tanks is that?
maths.answer: 2,880 litres in a day, which is nearly 3 rooftop tanks.
maths.explain: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so 2 times 60 is 120 litres an hour. 120 times 24 hours is 2,880 litres a day. 2,880 is a little less than 3,000, so it is nearly 3 tanks. The figure of 2 litres a minute is a made-up example inside the range that scientists have measured.
maths.context: In the Sea Soup test, you saw that a fine filter is slow. A sponge filters sea water all day to catch bacteria.
maths.why_maths: A food as thin as bacteria in sea water only feeds an animal who filters a huge amount, and multiplying shows how huge.

maths.problem: A stinging cell fires in about 700 billionths of a second. There are 1,000 million billionths in one second. About how many such firings, one after another, would fit into one second?
maths.explain: 1,000 million divided by 700 is the same as 10 million divided by 7, which is about 1.4 million. A blink of your eye takes about a third of a second, so roughly 470,000 firings would fit inside one blink.
maths.context: In the Inside-Out Thread, a balloon popped out of a bottle as a model of the thread in a stinging cell.
maths.why_maths: A time this short means nothing until you compare it with a time you know, such as a second or a blink.

maths.problem: In the Slow Sieve test, a tumbler of water took 4 seconds through the empty funnel and 80 seconds through firm cotton. How many times as long is that? If a pump pushed the water through the cotton in 20 seconds, how many times faster would that be than with no pump?
maths.answer: 20 times as long. With the pump, 4 times faster.
maths.explain: 80 divided by 4 is 20. So the fine gaps made the water take 20 times as long. 80 divided by 20 is 4, so the pump would make it 4 times faster than with no pump. Even then the water would be slower than through the empty neck, which is why the octopus has a second push after the gill.
maths.context: In the Slow Sieve test, you timed water running through a funnel with and without cotton packed in the neck.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by another turns 'much slower' into a number you can compare.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how people found out that sponges are animals, after thinking for a very long time that they were plants.
how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, most naturalists took sponges for plants. A sponge is fixed to a rock, grows in branches and does not pull away when touched. When Carl Linnaeus listed all living things in the 1700s, he first put sponges among the plants. A few people had seen water moving near sponges, but nobody knew what caused it. In the 1820s, Robert Grant, a doctor in Edinburgh in Scotland, collected living sponges from the sea shore near the city. In 1825 he put a small branch of one in a watch glass of sea water and looked through a microscope. He saw a strong stream of water pouring out of a round opening, carrying bits of waste with it. He called the sight a 'living fountain'. The stream came only from sponges that were alive and under water. So a sponge was pumping water through the body, taking food in and pushing waste out, which no plant does. In 1836 Grant gave the group the name Porifera, which means 'pore-bearers'.
how_we_found_out.who: Robert Grant, a Scottish doctor and naturalist
how_we_found_out.when: 1825, with the name Porifera given in 1836
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Sponges are plants, because they stay in one place and have branches. Grant showed that a living sponge pumps a stream of water through the body to feed, which is what an animal does.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1820s clothes bending over a microscope with a small branch of sponge in a watch glass, and a tiny jet of water with specks rising from the sponge.

playtest: Checked step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Boss or Hand test needs a big plate, 30 chana, a coin and a timer. Its result depends on the honest rule in Way 1, that the hand waits for an order even when the fingers feel the coin. Ordering every move should be clearly slowest. On a small plate the hand alone may match or beat 'aim only', and the last step tells the parent what to say then. A coin lying flat on steel is hard to pinch, so sliding it to the rim is allowed. Sea Soup stains the cloth yellow for good, so use an old one. The milk passes every filter and the water stays a little yellow, and the unit says so. The Slow Sieve needs a funnel or a cut bottle, which a grown-up cuts and tapes. A plug packed too tightly lets almost nothing through, and the step says to loosen it. In the Inside-Out Thread, the balloon goes into the bottle more easily if you squeeze the bottle a little, fit the balloon, and then let go. Feel or Taste needs both tumblers stirred until clear, or the grains give the answer away. Group Detective has 30 cards, 8 of them traps, and the highest score alone is 76. In the Field Book project most city families will find only arthropods and perhaps a snail alive, and that count is the finding. Facts were checked against web sources on 18 November 2026: the papers on octopus arms, suckers and hearts, the sponge sneeze, the speed of the stinging cell, Robert Grant and H. V. Wilson, the Indian law on sea cucumbers, the chank fishery, and the three videos.
